questions.stem: A weaning infant is diagnosed with an inherited enzyme deficiency that impairs fructose metabolism, and ingestion of fructose is causing progressive liver injury. The parents are counseled to eliminate dietary fructose. In addition to obvious fructose sources, which of the following dietary carbohydrates must they avoid because its digestion releases fructose?

explanation.summary: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, so its hydrolysis liberates free fructose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that sucrose (table sugar) is composed of glucose and fructose linked through both anomeric carbons. When digested, it releases fructose, which would be harmful to an infant unable to metabolize it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylose is a linear alpha-1,4 polymer of glucose only, with no fructose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cellulose is a beta-1,4 glucose polymer; it contains no fructose and is not digestible by humans.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactose is composed of galactose and glucose and contains no fructose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maltose is composed of two glucose molecules linked by an alpha-1,4 bond and contains no fructose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A researcher studies a membrane protein in the apical brush border of renal proximal tubule cells that moves glucose into the cell even when the intracellular glucose concentration exceeds that of the tubular lumen. This uphill transport is powered by an inwardly directed sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase. Which of the following transporters is being described?

explanation.summary: SGLT uses sodium symport to move glucose against its concentration gradient by secondary active transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that all GLUTs use facilitated diffusion except the sodium-glucose transporter (SGLT), which couples glucose uptake to a sodium gradient (secondary active transport) to reabsorb glucose in the proximal tubule and take up glucose/galactose from the intestinal lumen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 is a facilitated-diffusion transporter on RBCs and barrier tissues; it cannot move glucose against a gradient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT2 is a bidirectional facilitated transporter of liver, beta-cells, and basolateral enterocytes; it does not use sodium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT4 is an insulin-responsive facilitated transporter of muscle and adipose; it does not perform active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT5 is a facilitated fructose transporter and does not use a sodium gradient.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: In pancreatic beta-cells, a glucose transporter with a high Km and high Vmax allows glucose entry to track blood glucose concentration, so uptake rises sharply only when blood glucose is elevated. This behavior helps couple hyperglycemia to insulin secretion. Which transporter has these kinetic properties?

explanation.summary: GLUT2 has a high Km (low affinity) and high Vmax, matching the glucose-sensing role of the liver and pancreatic beta-cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that GLUT2's high relative Km means it only transports appreciably at high glucose concentrations, and its high Vmax and bidirectional flux fit the liver's role in blood glucose control and the beta-cell's role in sensing high glucose to release insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 has a low Km (high affinity) for basal uptake, not the high-Km sensing kinetics described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT3 has a low Km to preserve glucose for neurons, opposite of the described kinetics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 has a low Km and is insulin-responsive in muscle and adipose, not a high-Km beta-cell sensor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SGLT is a sodium-coupled active transporter of kidney and gut, not the beta-cell glucose sensor.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance is counseled that physical activity lowers blood glucose independently of insulin. During exercise, ATP is consumed and AMP accumulates, activating a cascade that increases glucose uptake into skeletal muscle. Which transporter is recruited to the plasma membrane by both insulin and this exercise-induced pathway?

explanation.summary: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive muscle/adipose transporter that is also recruited during exercise via AMP signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states GLUT4 is recruited to the membrane in response to insulin, and that exercise causes ATP expenditure and AMP accumulation, activating a cascade that also deposits GLUT4 on the cell surface. This insulin-independent route helps lower glucose when insulin resistance is present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 provides constitutive basal uptake and is not insulin- or exercise-recruited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT2 is a high-Km sensor of liver and beta-cells, not the muscle insulin-responsive transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT3 is the CNS neuronal transporter and is not recruited by insulin or exercise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT5 transports fructose in the intestine and sperm, unrelated to insulin-stimulated muscle uptake.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: Red blood cells lack mitochondria and depend entirely on glucose for energy, so they must take up glucose continuously even when a person is fasting and blood glucose is relatively low. Which property of the glucose transporter expressed on RBCs allows uptake to continue during fasting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high Km that limits uptake to high glucose levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: A low Km giving it high affinity for glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selective specificity for fructose over glucose

explanation.summary: GLUT1 on RBCs has a low Km (high affinity), so it binds and transports glucose even at low concentrations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that GLUT1, expressed on RBCs and barrier tissues, has a low Km (high affinity) and can transport glucose during times of fasting. Tissues that heavily rely on glucose express low-Km transporters mirroring high-affinity hexokinase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high Km would restrict uptake to high glucose levels, which is the GLUT2 pattern and would fail RBCs during fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT1 is not insulin-dependent; that describes GLUT4 in muscle and adipose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The RBC transporter carries glucose, not fructose; GLUT5 is the fructose transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sodium-coupled active transport is a feature of SGLT in kidney and gut, not the RBC transporter.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: Neurons can use only glucose for energy production, and the body prioritizes delivering glucose to the brain when circulating glucose is limited. The major central nervous system glucose transporter accomplishes this because it has a low Km for glucose. Which transporter is the major CNS transporter?

explanation.summary: GLUT3 is the major CNS neuronal transporter with a low Km (high affinity) that reserves scarce glucose for neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies GLUT3 as the major CNS transporter expressed on neurons, with a low relative Km for glucose, allowing low blood glucose to be reserved for neurons that can only use glucose for energy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 has a low Km but is described for RBCs and barrier tissues (including the blood-brain barrier), not as the neuronal CNS transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT2 is a high-Km sensor of liver and beta-cells, unsuitable for guaranteeing neuronal uptake at low glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive muscle/adipose transporter, not a neuronal transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT5 transports fructose in the intestine and sperm, not glucose in the CNS.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A 25-year-old develops bloating and diarrhea after drinking milk because of a brush-border enzyme deficiency. The offending sugar is a disaccharide of galactose and glucose. The brush-border enzyme normally hydrolyzes the specific glycosidic bond linking these two monosaccharides. Which glycosidic linkage joins the two sugars of this disaccharide?

explanation.summary: Lactose is galactose and glucose joined by a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond that lactase hydrolyzes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states lactose is made of galactose and glucose linked in a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond, and that human lactase hydrolyzes this beta-1,4 bond. Deficiency of this brush-border enzyme causes lactose intolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: alpha-1,2 is the linkage in sucrose (glucose-fructose), not lactose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: beta-1,3 is found in oat mucilage beta-glucan, not in lactose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: alpha-1,4 links the two glucose units of maltose, not galactose and glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: alpha-1,6 forms the branch points of amylopectin, not the lactose linkage.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: During a laboratory exercise, a student finds that glucose, maltose, and lactose all give a positive result in an assay that detects reducing sugars, but sucrose does not. Which structural feature best explains why sucrose is a nonreducing sugar?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both anomeric carbons are engaged in the glycosidic bond

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contains a ketose rather than an aldose unit

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a furanose rather than a pyranose ring

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is joined by a beta rather than an alpha linkage

explanation.summary: Sucrose is nonreducing because glucose and fructose are linked through both of their anomeric carbons, leaving no free anomeric carbon to be oxidized.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains a reducing sugar has a free anomeric carbon that can interconvert to the open-chain carbonyl and be oxidized. In sucrose, glucose and fructose are linked through both anomeric carbons (alpha-1,2), so neither can open to a carbonyl, making sucrose nonreducing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fructose is a ketose, but having a ketose unit does not prevent reduction; free fructose is a reducing sugar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sucrose is built from two hexoses, and carbon count does not determine reducing status.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ring size (furanose vs pyranose) does not determine reducing status; a free anomeric carbon does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bond stereochemistry (alpha vs beta) does not determine reducing status; lactose is beta-linked yet reducing.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A nutritionist explains that dietary cellulose passes through the gastrointestinal tract largely intact, providing bulk but minimal caloric value, whereas starch is readily digested to glucose. Both are polymers of glucose. What is the fundamental reason humans cannot digest cellulose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cellulose cannot be transported across enterocytes by GLUT2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cellulose is made of galactose rather than glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cellulose lacks a free anomeric carbon anywhere in the polymer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Humans lack an enzyme to cleave the beta-1,4 linkages between its glucose units

choices.label: E
choices.text: Salivary amylase is inactivated by the acidic stomach before reaching cellulose

explanation.summary: Humans lack the enzyme needed to hydrolyze cellulose's beta-1,4 glucose linkages, so it is indigestible.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick contrasts human lactase, which can hydrolyze the beta-1,4 bond of lactose, with cellulose, whose repeating beta-1,4 glucose linkages humans cannot cleave. Therefore cellulose has minimal nutritional value and moves through the gut as fiber.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The block is enzymatic hydrolysis, not transport; monosaccharides are never generated from cellulose to transport.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cellulose is a polymer of glucose, not galactose; the problem is the bond, not the monomer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reducing-end chemistry is not why cellulose is indigestible; the missing enzyme for beta-1,4 bonds is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amylase acts on starch's alpha-1,4 bonds; even a fully active amylase could not cleave cellulose's beta-1,4 bonds.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A modern glucometer uses glucose oxidase to convert glucose to gluconate, and the reaction is coupled to a signal read as glucose concentration. Because this enzymatic step is irreversible, nearly all of the blood glucose can be measured. Which principle explains why the irreversible reaction improves the measurement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates SGLT to concentrate glucose at the sensor

choices.label: B
choices.text: It converts the furanose ring to a more stable pyranose ring

choices.label: C
choices.text: It hydrolyzes glycosidic bonds to release additional glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents fructose in the sample from interfering with the reading

choices.label: E
choices.text: It pulls the equilibrium toward the open-chain aldehyde form

explanation.summary: Glucose oxidase irreversibly removes the open-chain form, shifting the equilibrium so essentially all glucose is pulled into the oxidizable open-chain aldehyde.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that glucose exists in equilibrium between cyclic and open-chain forms, and that the irreversible glucose oxidase step drives the equilibrium toward the open-chain aldehyde, so relatively all blood glucose is 'pulled' into the form that is oxidized and measured.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SGLT is an intestinal/renal transporter and plays no role in the glucometer chemistry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ring size conversion is not the mechanism; the assay depends on accessing the open-chain carbonyl.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose oxidase oxidizes glucose; it does not hydrolyze glycosidic bonds to liberate more glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The advantage is completeness of measurement via equilibrium shift, not exclusion of fructose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with chronic diarrhea and weight loss is evaluated for malabsorption. She is given an oral dose of a simple sugar that requires no digestive enzymes and is absorbed largely by passive diffusion across an intact mucosa without a dedicated transporter; blood and urine levels are then measured. Reduced absorption suggests mucosal damage. Which sugar is used in this test?

explanation.summary: The D-xylose test assesses intestinal mucosal integrity because D-xylose is absorbed by passive diffusion without needing enzymes or a transporter.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains the D-xylose test: D-xylose is a simple sugar that does not require digestive enzymes and is absorbed by passive diffusion across an intact mucosa, so measuring its blood and urine levels reflects mucosal integrity, with decreased absorption in mucosal damage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fructose requires the GLUT5 transporter for absorption, so it does not measure passive diffusion across the mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactose requires lactase and specific transport, and it tests for lactase deficiency, not general mucosal integrity by passive diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maltose is a disaccharide requiring maltase digestion and is not the passive-diffusion probe used clinically.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sucrose is a disaccharide requiring sucrase digestion, so it cannot test passive mucosal absorption directly.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: In a well-fed hepatocyte, glucose is abundant and glycolysis generates more acetyl-CoA than the TCA cycle can oxidize for immediate energy needs. Rather than being fully oxidized, this excess acetyl-CoA is diverted to store energy. Which of the following is an alternative fate of the excess acetyl-CoA?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reabsorption of glucose from the renal tubule

explanation.summary: Excess acetyl-CoA is channeled into lipogenesis, storing surplus glucose carbon as fat.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that abundant glucose in the liver can be used for the pentose phosphate pathway, glycogenesis, or fatty acid production, and that excess acetyl-CoA (not solely used as a TCA substrate) is stored as lipid via lipogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribose-5-phosphate is produced from glucose-6-phosphate in the pentose phosphate pathway, not from acetyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen is synthesized from glucose-6-phosphate, not from acetyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pentose phosphate pathway uses glucose-6-phosphate as substrate; acetyl-CoA does not enter it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal glucose reabsorption is an SGLT transport function, not a metabolic fate of acetyl-CoA.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A first-year student notes that carbohydrates share the general formula (CH2O)n and concludes they are literally "hydrates of carbon" with water molecules attached to carbon atoms. The instructor explains that this name is a misnomer. Which of the following is the most accurate functional description of a carbohydrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrated carbon atoms with water molecules attached

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polyhydroxy amines linked to amino acids

explanation.summary: Carbohydrates are best described functionally as polyhydroxy (many -OH groups) aldehydes or ketones.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states the name carbohydrate derives from the formula (CH2O)n, which only seems like a hydrate of carbon. A much better functional description is a polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone, and carbs are broadly classified as aldoses or ketoses depending on which carbonyl group they contain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Water is not literally attached to carbon; the formula only superficially resembles a hydrate, which is why the name is a misnomer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amines and amino acids are not part of the functional definition of a carbohydrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defining carbonyl of a carbohydrate is an aldehyde or ketone, not a carboxylic acid; a carboxylate (gluconate) appears only after oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphate esters are not part of the defining structure of a carbohydrate.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A biochemist examines the cyclic furanose form of D-fructose. Because fructose is a ketose, its carbonyl carbon is not carbon 1. When fructose cyclizes, which carbon becomes the anomeric carbon of the ring?

explanation.summary: The anomeric carbon is always the original carbonyl carbon, which is carbon 2 in a ketose such as fructose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the anomeric carbon is always the original carbon of the carbonyl from the aldehyde or ketone. For aldoses the #1 carbon is anomeric, and for ketoses it is the #2 carbon. In fructose the ketone is at carbon 2, so carbon 2 (C2 in Figure 2) is the anomeric carbon of fructofuranose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbon 1 is the anomeric carbon of aldoses like glucose; in fructose carbon 1 is a CH2OH group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbon 3 carries a hydroxyl group and is never the carbonyl carbon of fructose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbon 5 supplies the hydroxyl oxygen that closes the ring; it does not become the anomeric carbon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbon 6 is the terminal CH2OH of fructose, not a carbonyl carbon.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A student draws the cyclic pyranose form of D-glucose. In the drawing, the hydroxyl group attached to carbon 1 is positioned above the plane of the ring (drawn up). Which of the following correctly designates the structure that was drawn?

explanation.summary: A hydroxyl on the anomeric carbon drawn above the ring defines the beta anomer; below the ring defines alpha.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that anomeric carbons define carbohydrates as alpha or beta cyclic anomers: if the hydroxyl on the anomeric carbon is above the ring (drawn up) it is the beta anomer, while the alpha anomer has the hydroxyl in a downward position. Carbon 1 is the anomeric carbon of glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The alpha anomer has the anomeric hydroxyl pointing down (below the ring), the opposite of what was drawn.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A furanose is a five-membered ring; glucose in the pyranose form is a six-membered ring, and ring size is unrelated to the up/down hydroxyl orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A free monosaccharide with a free anomeric carbon is reducing; orientation of the hydroxyl does not make it nonreducing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The open-chain form has a free aldehyde and no ring, so there is no anomeric hydroxyl to orient.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: During cyclization of D-glucose into alpha-D-glucopyranose, an intramolecular reaction converts the carbon 1 aldehyde into a hemiacetal, and one hydroxyl oxygen becomes a member of the six-membered ring. The hydroxyl group on which carbon of open-chain glucose attacks the carbonyl to close the ring?

explanation.summary: In glucopyranose formation the carbon 5 hydroxyl oxygen bonds to the carbon 1 carbonyl, forming the ring oxygen and a hemiacetal at carbon 1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Figure 2 marks with an asterisk the oxygen that forms a new bond with the carbonyl to close the ring, and in D-glucose that oxygen is the hydroxyl on carbon 5. The aldehyde carbonyl reacts with it to form a hemiacetal (a carbon with an ether and an alcohol group), making carbon 1 the anomeric carbon and yielding a six-membered pyranose ring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbon 2 retains its hydroxyl in the ring form and does not supply the ring oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbon 3 retains its hydroxyl in the ring form and does not supply the ring oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbon 4 keeps its hydroxyl as a ring substituent; it is the site of linkage in 1,4 glycosidic bonds, not ring closure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The carbon 6 CH2OH remains outside the ring as a substituent in glucopyranose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A food chemist analyzes a carbohydrate additive and finds it consists of five sugar units joined by glycosidic bonds. According to standard carbohydrate nomenclature, this molecule is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Oligosaccharides contain several (about 3-7) sugar units.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines the terms by number of linked sugars: monosaccharides are single sugars, disaccharides have 2 units, oligosaccharides have several (~3-7) units, and polysaccharides have 8 or more units, usually reaching into the hundreds. A five-unit molecule falls in the oligosaccharide range.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A disaccharide contains exactly 2 sugar units.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycosaminoglycans are long, linear polysaccharides of repeating disaccharide units, far larger than five sugars.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A monosaccharide is a single simple sugar, not five linked units.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polysaccharides contain 8 or more sugar units, usually hundreds.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with coarse facial features and organomegaly is diagnosed with Hunter syndrome, a lysosomal enzyme deficiency classified as a mucopolysaccharidosis. The material that accumulates in his lysosomes is best described structurally as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Branched glucose polysaccharide with alpha-1,6 branch points

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disaccharide of galactose linked to glucose by a beta bond

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linear beta-1,4 polymer of many thousands of glucose units

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long linear polysaccharide of repeating disaccharide units

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oligosaccharide of three to seven linked fructose units

explanation.summary: Mucopolysaccharidoses cause accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, long linear polysaccharides composed of repeating disaccharide units.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that Hurler and Hunter syndromes are mucopolysaccharidoses, a term derived from polysaccharide. These lysosomal deficiencies cause accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, which are long, linear polysaccharides composed of repeating disaccharide units.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A branched alpha-1,6 glucose polymer describes amylopectin, a dietary plant starch, not a glycosaminoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A galactose-glucose disaccharide is lactose, a dietary sugar unrelated to lysosomal storage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A linear beta-1,4 glucose polymer is cellulose, a plant fiber that humans do not digest or store.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycosaminoglycans are polysaccharides, not oligosaccharides, and are not built from fructose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A synthetic disaccharide prescribed as a laxative is built from galactose and fructose. In its structure, the anomeric carbon of the galactose pyranose is oriented above the plane of its ring and is bonded to carbon 4 of a fructose furanose. Which of the following correctly names this glycosidic bond?

explanation.summary: Glycosidic bond names begin with the anomeric carbon in the link; a link above the ring plane is beta, so galactose C1 to fructose C4 is beta-1,4.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that glycosidic bonds are alpha (below the ring) or beta (above the ring), and the bond name includes which carbons are linked, with numbering starting from the anomeric carbon in the link. In lactulose the galactose anomeric carbon (#1) sits above the plane and joins fructose carbon 4, making a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bond joins carbon 4 of fructose, not carbon 2 (the fructose anomeric carbon, which remains free).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha would require the link to be below the plane of the ring containing the anomeric carbon; here it is above.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The connection is between carbons 1 and 4, not 1 and 6, and the orientation is beta, not alpha.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Numbering starts with the anomeric carbon of the link, so the bond is written 1,4 rather than 4,1.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: Two disaccharides each contain a fructose unit. In sucrose, glucose and fructose are joined through both of their anomeric carbons. In lactulose, galactose is joined through its anomeric carbon to carbon 4 of fructose, leaving the fructose anomeric carbon uninvolved in the bond. Which of the following correctly compares the two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are nonreducing because each contains fructose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both are reducing because each contains a ketose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactulose is reducing and sucrose is nonreducing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither can be classified because both are disaccharides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sucrose is reducing and lactulose is nonreducing

explanation.summary: A disaccharide is reducing only if one anomeric carbon remains free; lactulose keeps a free fructose anomeric carbon (a reducing end) whereas sucrose ties up both.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that reducing status is determined by the bonding state of the anomeric carbon: if it is free, the sugar can open to expose an oxidizable carbonyl. In lactulose the fructose anomeric carbon is not involved in the glycosidic link, so that end is a reducing end. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are locked in the alpha-1,2 bond, so it is nonreducing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Containing fructose does not make a sugar nonreducing; what matters is whether an anomeric carbon is free.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Having a ketose unit does not guarantee reducing status; sucrose contains fructose yet is nonreducing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reducing and nonreducing designations are specifically applied to disaccharides, oligosaccharides, and polysaccharides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is reversed: sucrose has no free anomeric carbon, and lactulose does.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: During nucleotide salvage, a purine base is attached to the #1 carbon of ribose through a glycosidic bond. A molecule in which a sugar is bound through a glycosidic bond to a non-sugar group such as a nitrogenous base, a protein, or a methyl group is designated by which general term?

explanation.summary: A glycoside is a sugar bound to another functional group via a glycosidic bond.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's critical note defines a glycoside as a molecule in which a sugar is bound to another functional group via a glycosidic bond, including simple groups like methyl or macromolecules like proteins, lipids, and nitrogenous bases. It cites N- and O-linked protein modification and purine/pyrimidine metabolism using a glycosidic link on ribose carbon 1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anomers are the alpha and beta ring forms defined by the anomeric hydroxyl orientation, not a bonded sugar-base compound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycosaminoglycans are long linear polysaccharides of repeating disaccharides, not a sugar joined to a non-sugar group.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An oligosaccharide is several sugar units linked to each other, not a sugar linked to a base or protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reducing sugar describes a free anomeric carbon; the anomeric carbon in a glycoside is tied up in the bond.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: Decades ago, an infant with an inherited disorder that caused a monosaccharide other than glucose to be excreted in the urine was labeled diabetic after a urine test for "sugar" was positive. Modern enzymatic testing later showed normal glucose. Which of the following best explains the original misdiagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial enzymes in the urine converted the sugar to glucose

choices.label: B
choices.text: The assay detected any reducing sugar rather than glucose specifically

choices.label: C
choices.text: The assay measured gluconate generated by glucose oxidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: The assay required so little sample that it was oversensitive

choices.label: E
choices.text: The excreted sugar was nonreducing and quenched the assay

explanation.summary: Older non-enzymatic sugar tests detected all reducing sugars, so disorders excreting other reducing sugars were misdiagnosed as diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that older blood glucose measurements were not enzyme based and employed chemistry to detect reducing sugars. Because the assay was not specific for glucose, disorders that caused other reducing sugars to be excreted were misdiagnosed as diabetes. All monosaccharides are reducing, so a non-glucose monosaccharide in urine gives a positive result.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes the error to assay nonspecificity, not to conversion of one sugar into glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose oxidase and gluconate formation are the basis of modern, glucose-specific glucometers, not the old chemistry-based test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The older tests actually required significantly more blood than modern tests; sample size did not cause the false diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: All monosaccharides are reducing sugars; a reducing sugar gives a positive result rather than quenching it.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: Red blood cells phosphorylate glucose using an enzyme that readily binds glucose even at low concentrations, and the kinetic properties of their glucose transporter mirror those of this enzyme. Which of the following correctly pairs the enzyme with the transporter kinetics found in RBCs?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose oxidase; GLUT with high Km

explanation.summary: RBCs express high-affinity (low Km) hexokinase, and their GLUT1 correspondingly has a low Km so glucose enters even during fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the kinetic features of GLUTs mirror the initial enzyme of glycolysis in that tissue. Hexokinase has high affinity (low Km) for glucose and is expressed by tissues that heavily rely on glucose, such as RBCs. It follows that GLUT1 on RBCs has a low Km (high affinity), so transport occurs even when circulating glucose is limited.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucokinase is the low-affinity, high-Km enzyme of liver and pancreatic islets, paired with high-Km GLUT2, not the RBC pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucokinase has a high Km, not a low one, and is not the RBC enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose oxidase is the enzyme used in glucometers, not a glycolytic enzyme expressed by RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hexokinase is correct, but a high-Km transporter would fail RBCs during fasting; GLUT1 has a low Km.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: Two plant starch polymers are digested by human amylases and disaccharidases. Amylose contains only alpha-1,4 linkages, whereas amylopectin also contains alpha-1,6 branches about every 24-30 glucose units. Digestion of amylopectin, but not amylose, is expected to yield which additional glucose disaccharide?

explanation.summary: Starch digestion yields maltose and isomaltose; isomaltose derives from the alpha-1,6 branch points unique to amylopectin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that amylose connects glucose linearly by alpha-1,4 links with no branching, while amylopectin has alpha-1,6 branches roughly every 24-30 glucose units, and that digestion gives rise to maltose and isomaltose, both glucose disaccharides. The alpha-1,4 linkages of both starches yield maltose, so the disaccharide that only amylopectin can contribute comes from its alpha-1,6 branch points, isomaltose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactose is galactose plus glucose from dairy, not a product of starch digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactulose is a synthetic galactose-fructose disaccharide used as a laxative, not a starch product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maltose (two glucoses in an alpha-1,4 bond) is produced from both amylose and amylopectin, so it is not unique to amylopectin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sucrose is glucose plus fructose from table sugar, not a product of starch digestion.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A carbohydrate isolated from potatoes is a polymer of glucose in which every unit is joined to the next by an alpha-1,4 link, forming a linear chain with no branching. Which of the following is this polysaccharide?

explanation.summary: Amylose is the unbranched plant starch built from glucose in alpha-1,4 linkages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the plant starches amylose and amylopectin found in staples like potatoes, rice, wheat, and corn. Amylose is the form that connects glucose linearly by alpha-1,4 links with no branching, whereas amylopectin adds alpha-1,6 branches.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylopectin has an amylose core plus alpha-1,6 branches about every 24-30 glucose units, so it is branched.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oat mucilage beta-glucan contains beta-1,3 linkages, not alpha-1,4 links.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cellulose is a linear glucose polymer, but its units are joined by beta-1,4 linkages that humans cannot digest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pectin is a soluble fiber, not an alpha-1,4 glucose starch.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A dietitian advises a patient with elevated cholesterol to increase intake of a type of dietary fiber that dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance and is abundant in oats, legumes, and fruits. Which of the following carbohydrates is an example of this fiber type?

explanation.summary: Pectin, gum, and mucilage are soluble fibers that dissolve in water to form a gel.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists pectin, gum, and mucilage as soluble fibers not digested by humans. Soluble fibers dissolve in water to form a gel-like substance, are found in oats, various legumes, and fruits, and offer the same health benefits described for cellulose, including reducing cholesterol and aiding blood glucose control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylopectin is a digestible branched starch, not a fiber.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amylose is a digestible starch that provides energy, not an indigestible soluble fiber.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cellulose is an insoluble fiber; it provides bulk but does not dissolve in water to form a gel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maltose is a digestible disaccharide (malt sugar) found in beer and bread, not a fiber.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A patient eating a high-oat diet is told that the beta-glucan in oat mucilage passes through the gastrointestinal tract without being broken down. Which of the following glycosidic linkages, present in this beta-glucan, is one that human digestive enzymes are unable to cleave?

explanation.summary: Oat mucilage beta-glucan contains beta-1,3 linkages that humans cannot break.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick gives beta-1,3 linkages routinely contained within the oat mucilage beta-glucan as an example of a bond humans are unable to break, alongside the beta-1,4 glucose linkages of cellulose. This is why such fibers are not digested.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1,2 is the sucrose linkage, which humans hydrolyze to glucose and fructose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1,4 glucose links are found in amylose, maltose, and amylopectin and are readily hydrolyzed by human amylases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-1,4 between galactose and glucose is the lactose bond, which human lactase can hydrolyze.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-1,6 branch links in amylopectin are digestible, yielding isomaltose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A nutrition researcher studies the composition of the average U.S. diet, in which carbohydrates supply 40-45% of total calories. Of the carbohydrate calories consumed, approximately what proportion comes from the plant starches amylose and amylopectin?

explanation.summary: Plant starches make up roughly 50-60% of carbohydrate calories consumed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the plant starches amylopectin and amylose constitute approximately 50% to 60% of the carbohydrate calories consumed, reflecting their abundance in staple foods like potatoes, rice, wheat, and corn. These polysaccharides contain 10,000 to 1 million glucosyl units.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This greatly underestimates the contribution of starch, which is the dominant dietary carbohydrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is well below the 50-60% figure given for starches.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is well below the 50-60% figure given for starches.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 40-45% is the share of total calories that all dietary carbohydrates provide, not the fraction of carbohydrate calories from starch.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops bloating and diarrhea after consuming dairy. Her physician explains that the enzyme responsible for hydrolyzing milk sugar, like the other critical disaccharidases, is produced by a specific cell type in her small intestine and that her cells are not producing enough of it. Which cells synthesize and release these disaccharidases?

explanation.summary: Disaccharidases are synthesized and released by brush border cells (enterocytes) of the small intestine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that the critical disaccharidases in the small intestine are synthesized and released by brush border cells, also known as enterocytes, whose apical microvilli increase surface area for absorption. The hydrolytic enzymes are secreted into the lumen to produce monosaccharides, so lactose intolerance originates in an inability of enterocytes to produce sufficient enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric cells are not described as a source of carbohydrate-digesting enzymes in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatocytes are involved in blood glucose control via GLUT2 and glucokinase, not in secreting digestive disaccharidases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pancreas contributes pancreatic alpha-amylase to the small intestine, not the brush border disaccharidases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salivary glands produce salivary alpha-amylase, which begins starch digestion, not disaccharidases.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin is released and recruits GLUT4 to the plasma membrane of adipocytes, increasing glucose uptake. Within the adipocyte, this glucose is used chiefly for which of the following purposes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct oxidation to gluconate for energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Export back to the plasma by bidirectional transport

choices.label: D
choices.text: Synthesis and storage of glycogen for later release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis of fatty acids and glycerol for TAG storage

explanation.summary: In adipose tissue, insulin-driven GLUT4 uptake supplies glucose for fatty acid and glycerol synthesis via glycolysis to store triacylglycerol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's GLUT table states that insulin increases glucose transport into adipose cells for synthesis of fatty acids and glycerol by glycolysis for TAG storage. In contrast, insulin increases glucose transport into skeletal muscle for glycolysis and glycogen storage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxidation of glucose to gluconate is the glucose oxidase reaction in glucometers, not a cellular energy pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bidirectional transport allowing glucose export is a property of hepatic GLUT2, not adipocyte GLUT4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pentose phosphate pathway is listed as a hepatic fate of abundant glucose, not the adipocyte's principal use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycolysis and glycogen storage is the fate described for glucose entering skeletal muscle, not adipose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A patient trying to greatly reduce fructose intake for health reasons continues drinking soda but switches from a version sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup to an imported version sweetened with cane sugar (sucrose), reasoning that it contains sucrose instead of fructose. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Effective, because sucrose contains no fructose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Effective, because sucrose is not digested by humans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Effective, because the fructose in sucrose is nonreducing and unabsorbed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ineffective, because sucrose is digested into two fructose molecules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ineffective, because sucrose is itself 50% fructose

explanation.summary: Sucrose is composed of 50% fructose, so swapping high-fructose corn syrup for cane sugar would not significantly reduce fructose consumption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case conclusion notes that while the sweeteners are distinct, sucrose is comprised of 50% fructose (one glucose plus one fructose). While some high-fructose corn syrup formulas are higher than that, the proposed strategy would likely not reduce fructose consumption significantly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, so it does contain fructose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Humans readily digest sucrose with brush border disaccharidases; cellulose is the undigestible glucose polymer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sucrose is nonreducing as an intact disaccharide, but it is hydrolyzed and its fructose is absorbed via GLUT5.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sucrose yields one glucose and one fructose, not two fructose molecules.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: After a meal, glucose, galactose, and fructose are taken up across the apical membrane of intestinal enterocytes by two different transporters. All three monosaccharides then leave the enterocyte across the basolateral membrane to enter the bloodstream. Which transporter mediates this basolateral exit?

explanation.summary: GLUT2 on the basolateral surface of enterocytes moves absorbed glucose, galactose, and fructose into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's absorption figure shows SGLT1 (glucose or galactose with Na+) and GLUT5 (fructose) on the apical membrane, and all three sugars exiting through GLUT2 on the basolateral membrane. The GLUT table lists GLUT2's digestive role as the basolateral surface of intestinal enterocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 is expressed on RBCs and barrier tissues, not described as the enterocyte basolateral exporter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT1 is the apical sodium-coupled transporter that brings glucose or galactose in from the lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose, not enterocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT5 is the apical fructose transporter of the intestinal luminal epithelium.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: An experimental toxin selectively inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase on the basolateral membrane of intestinal enterocytes, collapsing the sodium gradient across the apical membrane. Uptake of which of the following sugars from the intestinal lumen would be most directly impaired?

explanation.summary: SGLT1 uptake of glucose and galactose depends on the sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase; fructose enters by facilitated diffusion via GLUT5.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure shows SGLT1 on the apical membrane moving Na+ together with glucose or galactose, powered by the Na+/K+ ATPase pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in on the basolateral side. Without this gradient, secondary active transport of glucose and galactose fails. Fructose enters through GLUT5 by facilitated diffusion, which does not require sodium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: D-xylose is absorbed by passive diffusion without a transporter, so it is unaffected by loss of the sodium gradient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Galactose uptake would be impaired, but fructose enters independently of sodium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fructose uptake by GLUT5 is facilitated diffusion and does not depend on the sodium gradient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose uptake would be impaired, but fructose enters independently of sodium.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A researcher characterizes glucose transporters in the placenta, retina, testis, and the endothelium of the blood-brain barrier, all tissues that share a barrier function. Which transporter would be expected to predominate at these sites?

explanation.summary: GLUT1 is expressed on RBCs and on cells with barrier function, including brain, retina, placenta, and testis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's GLUT table lists the tissue distribution of GLUT1 as RBC and cells with barrier function (brain, retina, placenta, testis), with a low Km for glucose (high affinity) allowing transport during fasting.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT2 is expressed on the basolateral enterocyte surface, liver, and pancreatic beta-cells, not barrier tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT3 is the major CNS transporter on neurons themselves, not the barrier tissues listed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT5 transports fructose in the intestinal luminal epithelium and sperm.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: During an overnight fast, the liver releases glucose into the circulation to maintain blood glucose. The hepatocyte glucose transporter accommodates this reversal of glucose flow. Which property of the hepatic transporter allows glucose to leave the hepatocyte during fasting?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low Km giving high glucose affinity

explanation.summary: Hepatic GLUT2 is bidirectional, allowing glucose export from the liver in times of fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's GLUT table states that GLUT2 in liver is bidirectional to allow glucose export in times of fasting, in addition to its high Km and high transport capacity that let it take up glucose only when circulating levels are high.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin-dependent recruitment describes GLUT4 in muscle and adipose, and insulin is low during fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT2 has a high relative Km (low affinity); a low Km describes GLUT1, GLUT3, and GLUT4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sodium symport is the mechanism of SGLT in kidney and gut, which concentrates glucose inward rather than exporting it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fructose specificity describes GLUT5; the hepatic transporter handles glucose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A pharmacology student compares the kinetic properties of the fructose transporter of the intestinal luminal epithelium and sperm with those of the other medically relevant glucose transporters. Relative to GLUT1 and GLUT2, the Km of this fructose transporter is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Between those of GLUT1 and GLUT2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equal to the low Km of GLUT1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Equal to the high Km of GLUT2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher than that of both GLUT1 and GLUT2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lower than that of both GLUT1 and GLUT2

explanation.summary: GLUT5 has a moderate affinity, with a Km value between that of GLUT1 and GLUT2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's GLUT table describes GLUT5, the fructose transporter in intestinal luminal epithelium and sperm, as having a Km value between that of GLUT1 and GLUT2 (moderate affinity). It also notes that fructose can be transported by other GLUTs as well.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT5's Km is intermediate, not equal to the low Km of GLUT1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT5's Km is intermediate, not equal to the high Km of GLUT2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT2 has the high relative Km (low affinity); GLUT5's Km does not exceed it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT1 has a low Km (high affinity); GLUT5's affinity is only moderate, so its Km is not lower than GLUT1's.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated because his parents noticed he does not track objects well and has cloudiness of both eyes. Examination reveals bilateral cataracts. He is growing and developing normally, has no hepatomegaly, and has met his cognitive milestones. Urinalysis reveals reducing substances and elevated galactose. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: Isolated cataracts with elevated galactose and no systemic disease indicate galactokinase deficiency (type II galactosemia).
explanation.whyCorrect: Galactokinase deficiency is a mild disorder in which galactose-1-phosphate is never formed, so patients lack hepatic and neurologic disease. Excess galactose is instead shunted to galactitol by aldose reductase; galactitol accumulates in the lens and causes cataracts, which are often the only manifestation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldose reductase is the enzyme that produces galactitol; it is not deficient here and its loss would prevent, not cause, cataracts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GALT deficiency is classic (type I) galactosemia and causes severe hepatomegaly, jaundice, failure to thrive, and intellectual disability, not isolated cataracts in a well-developing child.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactase deficiency causes gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea and bloating, not cataracts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GALE deficiency (type III) is rare, and its severity is generally similar to classic galactosemia, not a mild isolated-cataract picture.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 6-day-old exclusively breastfed girl presents with poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show hypoglycemia and urinary reducing substances that are not glucose. She subsequently develops Escherichia coli sepsis. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: A breastfed neonate with jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and E. coli sepsis has classic (type I) galactosemia from GALT deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In classic galactosemia the deficient enzyme is GALT, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and is toxic, producing hepatomegaly, jaundice, failure to thrive, and hypoglycemia within days of milk (lactose) feeding. Excess galactose within neutrophils impairs their bactericidal activity, predisposing the neonate to E. coli sepsis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) is triggered by fructose or sucrose on weaning to fruits, not by lactose in breast milk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldose reductase produces galactitol and is not a primary deficiency disorder; it does not explain hepatic failure and sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galactokinase deficiency is mild, causing isolated cataracts without liver disease or sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhea, not hepatomegaly, jaundice, and sepsis.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: Both galactokinase deficiency and classic galactosemia can cause cataracts even though galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in only one of them. Which of the following is the direct biochemical cause of the lens opacity shared by both disorders?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of excess galactose to galactitol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of galactose-1-phosphate within lens fibers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycation of crystallin proteins by free galactose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Primary deficiency of glutathione peroxidase in the lens

explanation.summary: Cataracts in galactose disorders result from galactitol produced by aldose reductase, which causes osmotic and oxidative stress in the lens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excess galactose is reduced to galactitol by aldose reductase in the lens. Galactitol cannot be further metabolized or exported, so it accumulates and draws in water (osmotic stress); its production also consumes NADPH, lowering reduced glutathione and adding oxidative stress. Together these denature and aggregate lens proteins, producing opacity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: UDP-galactose accumulation relates to GALE and is not the lens cataract mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galactose-1-phosphate does not accumulate in galactokinase deficiency, yet cataracts still occur, so the shared cause must be galactitol, not galactose-1-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycation of crystallins is not the mechanism described in the source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The problem is reduced NADPH supply for glutathione, not a primary glutathione peroxidase deficiency.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: Aldose reductase converts galactose to galactitol in patients with galactosemia but is essentially inactive under normal physiologic conditions. Which of the following properties best explains why this enzyme becomes active only when galactose is in excess?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has a very high Km (low affinity) for galactose

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has a very low Km (high affinity) for galactose

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is competitively inhibited by NADPH

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is expressed only during the fasting state

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires ATP that is depleted at normal galactose levels

explanation.summary: Aldose reductase has a very high Km, so it only produces galactitol when galactose accumulates to high levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: A very high Km means low substrate affinity, so at normal galactose concentrations the enzyme is nearly inactive. Only when galactose accumulates (as in galactosemia) does the substrate concentration approach the Km, allowing the enzyme to generate galactitol while consuming NADPH.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A low Km (high affinity) enzyme such as galactokinase works efficiently at low substrate concentrations, which is the opposite of aldose reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NADPH is the cofactor consumed by the reaction, not an inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its activity is driven by substrate concentration, not by the fasting state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aldose reductase uses NADPH, not ATP.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: Glycogen consists of glucose residues joined into linear chains with periodic branches. Which of the following linkages is found specifically at the branch points?

explanation.summary: Glycogen branch points are formed by alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The linear core of glycogen is linked by alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds, while branch points, which occur every 8 to 12 residues, are created by alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds. This branching produces glycogen's highly branched architecture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1,1 links glucose units in trehalose, not in glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-1,4 bonds form the linear chains, not the branch points.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-1,4 linkages are found in cellulose and lactose, not in glycogen branches.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-1,6 is not the glycogen branch linkage.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: The highly branched structure of glycogen is advantageous in exercising muscle or in the fasting liver. Which of the following features of branching most directly permits rapid mobilization of glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows glucose to diffuse out of the polymer without enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It creates many non-reducing ends where degradative enzymes act

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases the number of reducing ends attached to glycogenin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reduces the total number of glucose molecules that can be stored

choices.label: E
choices.text: It strengthens alpha-1,6 bonds against hydrolysis

explanation.summary: Branching multiplies non-reducing ends, allowing many enzymes to release glucose at once.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each branch adds a non-reducing end, and degradative enzymes act on non-reducing ends. Numerous branches therefore let many enzyme molecules liberate glucose simultaneously, greatly increasing the rate of release. A linear polymer would offer only a single such site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose release requires enzymatic cleavage of the polymer, not free diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is only one reducing end (attached to glycogenin); branching multiplies non-reducing ends, not reducing ends.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Branching organizes the same amount of glucose for faster access and does not reduce how much is stored.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Branching does not make bonds resistant to hydrolysis; the benefit is faster degradation, not stability.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: Cells store glucose as glycogen rather than as free glucose molecules. Storing the same total quantity of glucose as free monosaccharides instead of polymerized glycogen would most likely cause which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An increase in blood glucose osmolarity only

choices.label: D
choices.text: Massive osmotic water influx and cell swelling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Precipitation of glucose crystals within the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: Polymerizing glucose into glycogen minimizes osmotically active particles, preventing water influx.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combining many glucose units into one large glycogen molecule greatly reduces the number of osmotically active particles inside the cell. The same amount of glucose as free monosaccharides would raise intracellular osmolarity and draw water in to balance osmolality, swelling and distorting the tissue and compromising function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The osmotic stress is intracellular, not limited to the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Storing free glucose does not by itself deplete ATP; the concern is osmosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stress described is osmotic, not a change in pH or acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose remains in solution and does not precipitate as crystals.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant has hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and progressive liver cirrhosis. A liver biopsy shows abnormally structured glycogen with a normal core but absent branches, along with chronic hepatic inflammation. The condition is usually fatal within about 2 years. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: Unbranched glycogen with hepatic inflammation and early fatal cirrhosis is Andersen disease (type IV GSD), a branching enzyme deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Andersen disease the branching enzyme is deficient, so the glycogen core forms but branches fail. The abnormally structured glycogen is perceived by the immune system as foreign, causing chronic hepatic inflammation, cirrhosis, and death typically within about 2 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galactokinase deficiency causes cataracts, not this hepatic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, not unbranched glycogen with cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Debranching enzyme deficiency (Cori disease) produces glycogen with short outer branches rather than absent branches, and it is generally milder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe disease) causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation with cardiomegaly and hypotonia.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: An adult with lactase deficiency develops bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea after drinking milk. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the watery diarrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the intestinal villi and brush border

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct toxicity of undigested lactose to the enterocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased SGLT-mediated glucose absorption across the brush border

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmotically active lactic acid from bacterial fermentation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pancreatic enzyme insufficiency with impaired starch digestion

explanation.summary: Undigested lactose is fermented by gut bacteria to osmotically active lactic acid, which draws water into the lumen and triggers diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because lactase is deficient, lactose remains in the gut lumen where bacteria ferment it into gas (CO2, methane) plus lactic acid and other byproducts. The gas causes bloating and flatulence, while the osmotically active lactic acid pulls water into the lumen, distending the intestinal wall and triggering powerful peristalsis that produces watery diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactose intolerance is not an autoimmune villous destruction, which characterizes celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactose is not directly toxic to enterocytes; the problem is luminal fermentation and osmosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absorption is decreased, not increased; uncleaved lactose does not liberate glucose and galactose for SGLT uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pancreas and its enzymes are normal in lactose intolerance.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A newborn develops severe watery diarrhea, weight loss, and dehydration within days of starting breast milk. The symptoms resolve completely when a lactose-free formula is substituted. The disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A severe autosomal recessive newborn diarrhea that resolves with lactose removal is congenital lactase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital lactase deficiency is a severe autosomal recessive disorder with markedly reduced or absent lactase from birth. It presents as soon as the newborn is fed breast milk or lactose-containing formula, with watery diarrhea, weight loss, and dehydration, and removing lactose from the diet restores normal growth and development.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult-type hypolactasia develops later in childhood or adulthood as lactase levels decline, not in a newborn.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Andersen disease causes progressive liver failure and cirrhosis, not diarrhea that resolves with a formula change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Classic galactosemia causes systemic disease such as jaundice, hepatomegaly, and hypoglycemia rather than isolated osmotic diarrhea that resolves cleanly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hereditary fructose intolerance presents when fructose or sucrose is introduced on weaning to fruits, not with breast milk.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A gastroenterologist wants to confirm carbohydrate malabsorption noninvasively. The patient ingests a specific test sugar, and exhaled breath is analyzed over time. Detection of which of the following gases indicates bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed sugar?

explanation.summary: The hydrogen breath test detects hydrogen, methane, or hydrogen sulfide produced by bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed sugar.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the hydrogen breath test, a patient consumes a specific carbohydrate and breath samples are analyzed for hydrogen, methane, or hydrogen sulfide. Elevated gas content indicates that undigested or unabsorbed sugars are being fermented by gut bacteria, supporting diagnoses such as lactose intolerance, SIBO, or fructose malabsorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ammonia is not the gas measured in this diagnostic test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbon monoxide is not the bacterial fermentation product measured in this test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide is not the gas assayed by the hydrogen breath test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxygen and nitrogen are normal components of air and are not fermentation markers.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: In classic galactosemia, affected infants develop fasting hypoglycemia. Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate contributes to this hypoglycemia by which of the following pairs of mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating insulin secretion and causing glucagon resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depleting ATP and inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating aldose reductase and glycogen synthase

explanation.summary: Galactose-1-phosphate traps phosphate to deplete ATP and inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, impairing glucose output and causing hypoglycemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the first step (galactokinase) is intact in GALT deficiency, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and depleting ATP, which impairs ATP-dependent hepatic gluconeogenesis. High galactose-1-phosphate also inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, blocking the first step of glycogen degradation. Both effects reduce hepatic glucose output, producing fasting hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mechanism is metabolic enzyme inhibition and ATP depletion, not altered insulin or glucagon signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis are impaired, not enhanced, in classic galactosemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hexokinase inhibition and glucose-6-phosphatase activation are not the mechanisms described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aldose reductase produces galactitol (cataracts) and does not raise blood glucose, and stimulating glycogen synthase would not explain reduced glucose output.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 30-year-old marathon runner is studied during a prolonged fast followed by exercise. Investigators compare the fate of glycogen stored in his liver with that stored in his skeletal muscle. Which of the following best describes the difference between these two glycogen depots?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liver glycogen is degraded only during exercise, whereas muscle glycogen is degraded only during fasting

choices.label: B
choices.text: Liver glycogen is exported as free glucose for other tissues, whereas muscle glycogen is used by muscle alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver glycogen is linked by beta-1,4 bonds, whereas muscle glycogen is linked by alpha-1,4 bonds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liver glycogen is used only by hepatocytes, whereas muscle glycogen is exported to other tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Liver glycogen lacks branch points, whereas muscle glycogen is highly branched

explanation.summary: The liver liberates and exports glucose from glycogen for other tissues, while skeletal muscle glycogen is consumed only by the muscle that stores it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycogen is contained within both the liver and skeletal muscle and serves as a depot for excess glucose. The liver liberates and exports individual glucose molecules derived from glycogen to support metabolism in other tissues. In contrast, glycogen stored within skeletal muscle is utilized by skeletal muscle alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both depots can be mobilized in exercise or fasting; the distinction is who uses the released glucose, not the timing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen in every tissue uses alpha-1,4 linkages in its chains; beta-1,4 bonds are not part of glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the roles: it is the liver, not muscle, that exports glucose for other tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogen in both tissues is a highly branched polymer with the same alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 architecture.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is diagramming the architecture of a glycogen molecule. She draws a linear chain of glucose residues and needs to indicate how frequently alpha-1,6 branch points occur along the chain. Approximately how many glucose units separate successive branch points in glycogen?

explanation.summary: Glycogen branches occur every 8-12 glucose units along the alpha-1,4-linked chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycogen has a linear core of glucose linked via alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds with branching occurring every 8 to 12 glucose units. This frequent branching creates the highly branched structure that provides multiple non-reducing ends for rapid glucose release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Branching every 1-2 residues is far too frequent; glycogen chains run 8-12 residues between branches.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Branching every 3-5 residues is more frequent than the 8-12 units described for glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Branching every 20-30 residues is too sparse to generate the many non-reducing ends that glycogen contains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Branches every 50-100 residues would make glycogen nearly linear, not highly branched.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: In a glycogen molecule, a branch is initiated when a glucose residue is attached to the core through an alpha-1,6 glycosidic bond. Which of the following linkages joins the subsequent glucose residues to one another within that branch, beyond the branch point?

explanation.summary: Only the branch point itself is an alpha-1,6 bond; residues within a branch are connected again by alpha-1,4 bonds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The branch points of glycogen uniquely contain alpha-1,6 glycosidic links, but the subsequent glucose residues within each branch are connected again by alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds, just like the linear core. Thus alpha-1,6 bonds occur only once per branch, at its origin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1,2 bonds are not part of glycogen structure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-1,4 bonds are not found anywhere in glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-1,6 bonds are unique to the branch point itself, not to the chain continuing beyond it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-1,6 bonds are not part of glycogen structure.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A research group isolates a single intact glycogen granule and maps its terminal residues. They identify hundreds of non-reducing ends distributed across the branches. When they search for the reducing end of the polymer, which of the following do they most likely find?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A free reducing end for each 8-12 residue segment

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reducing end at each alpha-1,6 branch point

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single reducing end attached to the protein glycogenin

choices.label: D
choices.text: No reducing end, because all ends are non-reducing

choices.label: E
choices.text: One reducing end at the tip of every branch

explanation.summary: Glycogen has one reducing end, which is attached to glycogenin, while all branch tips are non-reducing ends.
explanation.whyCorrect: The glycogen molecule is built outward from a single reducing end that is attached to the protein glycogenin. Every branch terminates in a non-reducing end, and it is these numerous non-reducing ends that degradative enzymes act on simultaneously to release glucose rapidly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 8-12 residue spacing describes branch frequency, not the number of reducing ends; there is only one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Branch points are alpha-1,6 linkages within the polymer, not reducing ends.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycogen does have a reducing end; it is anchored to glycogenin rather than free.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Branch tips are non-reducing ends, which is why they serve as the sites for enzymatic glucose release.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy with a branching enzyme deficiency has progressive hepatic dysfunction. Liver biopsy shows glycogen with a normal linear core but no branches, accompanied by chronic hepatic inflammation. Which of the following best explains why the abnormal glycogen leads to chronic liver inflammation in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycogen phosphorylase is inhibited by the unbranched polymer and traps phosphate

choices.label: B
choices.text: The abnormally structured glycogen is perceived by the immune system as a foreign body

choices.label: C
choices.text: The unbranched polymer is fermented by gut bacteria into lactic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unbranched glycogen is converted to galactitol that osmotically swells hepatocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unbranched glycogen releases glucose too rapidly and causes hepatocyte hyperglycemia

explanation.summary: In Andersen disease, the abnormal unbranched glycogen is recognized as foreign, provoking an immune response and chronic hepatic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Andersen disease (type IV GSD) results from branching enzyme deficiency: the glycogen core forms but branches fail. The resulting liver dysfunction is largely due to an immune response, because the abnormal glycogen structure is perceived as a foreign body, creating chronic hepatic inflammation that progresses to advanced cirrhosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phosphate trapping and glycogen phosphorylase inhibition are mechanisms of hypoglycemia in classical galactosemia, not Andersen disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen is intracellular; bacterial fermentation of luminal sugars is the mechanism of lactose intolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Galactitol is produced from galactose by aldose reductase in galactosemia; it has nothing to do with glycogen structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A linear polymer has only a single site from which to release glucose, so mobilization is slower, not faster.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A pediatric hepatologist explains to parents that their child's fatal liver disease belongs to a family of inherited disorders caused by deficiencies of the specialized enzymes that form and destroy glycogen. The child's specific defect is in the branching enzyme. Which of the following is the correct classification of this child's disorder?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type I glycogen storage disease (von Gierke)

explanation.summary: Branching enzyme deficiency is Andersen disease, classified as type IV glycogen storage disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Specialized enzymes within skeletal muscle and liver form (branching enzymes) and destroy (debranching enzymes) glycogen. Deficiency of these enzymes falls under the class of disorders known as glycogen storage diseases (GSD). Andersen disease, caused by branching enzyme deficiency, is type IV GSD and is usually fatal within 2 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I galactosemia is GALT deficiency, a disorder of galactose metabolism rather than glycogen structure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I GSD is not the branching enzyme deficiency; Andersen disease is specifically type IV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type II galactosemia is galactokinase deficiency, which causes cataracts, not fatal liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type III galactosemia is GALE deficiency, unrelated to glycogen branching.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia
