questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with adult hypolactasia drinks a large milkshake and within a few hours develops marked abdominal bloating and flatulence, followed later by watery diarrhea. Which of the following bacterial products is most directly responsible for her bloating and flatulence?

explanation.summary: Gases such as CO2 and CH4 released by bacterial fermentation of lactose cause bloating and flatulence, whereas lactic acid drives the osmotic diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: When lactase is deficient, lactose remains in the gut lumen for bacterial metabolism. Bacteria feeding on lactose release gases such as CO2 and CH4, along with lactic acid and other byproducts. The gas results in bloating and flatulence, while the osmotically active lactic acid draws water into the lumen and produces watery diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose and galactose are the products of normal lactase cleavage and are absorbed via SGLT; they are not generated in lactase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galactitol is formed from excess galactose by aldose reductase in galactosemia; it is not a product of gut bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Galactose 1-phosphate is the intracellular toxic metabolite of classical galactosemia, unrelated to luminal fermentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactic acid is osmotically active and causes the water influx and diarrhea, not the gaseous distention.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A healthy infant with normal lactase activity drinks breast milk. Lactose in the milk is cleaved into its component monosaccharides at the intestinal brush border. Which of the following transporters then carries those monosaccharides into the intestinal wall?

explanation.summary: After lactase cleaves lactose into glucose and galactose, the monosaccharides are absorbed into the intestinal wall via SGLT.
explanation.whyCorrect: When lactose is ingested it is normally cleaved into the monosaccharides glucose and galactose by the lactase enzyme, with subsequent absorption into the intestinal wall via SGLT. Only when lactase is deficient does lactose remain in the lumen for bacterial metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldose reductase is an enzyme that converts excess galactose to galactitol; it is not a transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose inside cells after absorption; it is not a membrane transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT4 is not the transporter named for intestinal absorption of the products of lactose digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactose synthase is the mammary enzyme that builds lactose from UDP-galactose and glucose; it does not absorb sugars.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A pediatrician counsels the parents of a healthy 2-year-old about typical lactase expression over the lifespan. In an average person, lactase levels stay high for about a month after birth and then decline steadily. At approximately what age does lactase activity typically reach the residual level (less than 10% of infant levels) that persists throughout adulthood?

explanation.summary: Lactase expression declines steadily after the first month of life until about age 5, when it falls below 10% of infant levels and stays there through adulthood.
explanation.whyCorrect: In most individuals, lactase expression increases during gestation and remains high for about 1 month after birth to ensure proper digestion of milk. Expression then begins to decline fairly steadily until about age 5, when levels become less than 10% of those present in infants. This is the typical residual activity an individual will have throughout adulthood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At 1 year lactase is still declining and remains above the less-than-10% adult level.
whyWrongByChoice.C: At 6 months the decline has only begun; levels have not yet reached the adult residual value.
whyWrongByChoice.D: By 12 years lactase has long since reached its residual level; the plateau is reached around age 5.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adult residual activity is established in early childhood, not in the third decade.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: An epidemiologist compares the prevalence of adult lactase deficiency across populations. She notes that genetic ancestry greatly influences adult lactase expression: individuals of Native Indian descent in Oklahoma have an incidence of adult lactase deficiency above 95%. Which of the following populations is described as having the lowest prevalence of lactose intolerance, at less than 3%?

explanation.summary: Danish and Dutch populations exhibit lactose intolerance in less than 3% of individuals, contrasting with more than 95% in Native Indian descent in Oklahoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The majority of the world's population is lactose intolerant to some degree, and genetic ancestry greatly influences adult lactase expression. Individuals of Native Indian genetic descent in Oklahoma have a very high incidence of adult lactase deficiency (>95%), whereas Danish and Dutch populations exhibit less than 3% on average of individuals with lactose intolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: East Asian populations are not the group cited as having the under-3% prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mediterranean populations are not the group cited as having the under-3% prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: South American populations are not the group cited as having the under-3% prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: West African populations are not the group cited as having the under-3% prevalence.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic bloating and diarrhea is suspected of having small intestine bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). His physician orders a non-invasive test in which the patient ingests a specific carbohydrate and then provides breath samples over time. Which of the following best describes what this test measures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exhaled carbon dioxide produced by hepatic oxidation of the ingested carbohydrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exhaled hydrogen, methane, or hydrogen sulfide from bacterial fermentation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum galactose 1-phosphate measured after an oral lactose load

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stool lactic acid concentration measured after an oral lactose load

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary reducing substances measured after an oral galactose load

explanation.summary: The hydrogen breath test detects fermentation gases in exhaled breath and is used for SIBO as well as lactose intolerance and fructose malabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hydrogen breath test is a non-invasive diagnostic tool used to identify various gastrointestinal conditions, including lactose intolerance, SIBO, and carbohydrate malabsorption such as with fructose. The patient consumes a specific carbohydrate and breath samples are analyzed over time for hydrogen, methane, or hydrogen sulfide; elevated gas content indicates that undigested or unabsorbed sugars are being fermented by gut bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gases measured come from bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed sugar in the gut, not hepatic oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galactose 1-phosphate is the intracellular metabolite of classical galactosemia, not a breath-test analyte.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The test analyzes exhaled gas, not stool; lactic acid is the osmotic byproduct, not what is measured.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary reducing substances are relevant to galactosemia, not to a breath test for bacterial fermentation.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A dietitian counsels the parents of a 3-year-old girl with classical galactosemia who has been on a strict dairy-free diet since newborn screening. The parents ask which additional non-dairy foods must also be avoided because they contain galactose. Which of the following foods should the dietitian identify?

explanation.summary: Beyond dairy, galactose sources include organ meats (pancreas, liver) and chickpeas (garbanzo beans), which must be eliminated in galactosemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elimination of galactose-containing foods, primarily dairy products, is the mainstay of treatment for galactose metabolism disorders. Other sources include organ meat such as pancreas and liver, and chickpeas (garbanzo beans). A lactose- and galactose-free diet prevents all complications related to the enzyme deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Muscle meat and eggs are not listed as galactose sources; the concern is organ meats such as liver and pancreas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Citrus fruits and honey are sources of fructose and sucrose, which are relevant to fructose disorders, not galactosemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Starchy staples such as potatoes and rice are not identified as galactose sources.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wheat products are not identified as galactose sources in the dietary guidance for galactosemia.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A radiolabeled galactose tracer is administered to a healthy volunteer, and investigators measure where the majority of the tracer is metabolized. Which of the following organs predominantly metabolizes dietary galactose?

explanation.summary: The liver predominantly metabolizes galactose, with the intestines and kidney contributing to a lesser extent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humans primarily obtain galactose in the form of lactose from milk and dairy products, including breast milk and most infant formulas. The liver predominantly metabolizes galactose, while to a lesser extent the intestines and kidney also metabolize it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brain is a site of damage from galactitol accumulation, not the primary site of galactose metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney metabolizes galactose only to a lesser extent than the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lens receives spillover galactose and forms galactitol via aldose reductase; it does not carry out the main metabolic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle is a glycogen storage site but is not described as a site of galactose metabolism.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: An enzymologist characterizes galactokinase, the first enzyme of galactose metabolism, and finds that it phosphorylates galactose rapidly even at low substrate concentrations. Which of the following combinations of kinetic properties and cofactor requirements best describes galactokinase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High Km, high Vmax, consumes ATP

choices.label: B
choices.text: High Km, low Vmax, consumes NADPH

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low Km, high Vmax, consumes ATP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low Km, high Vmax, consumes UDP-glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low Km, low Vmax, consumes NADPH

explanation.summary: Galactokinase is a highly efficient, high-affinity (low Km), high-Vmax enzyme that uses ATP to make galactose 1-phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Galactokinase is a highly efficient enzyme that converts galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. It has a fairly low Km (high affinity) but a high Vmax, and the step consumes ATP to provide the phosphorylated galactose. Because this first step is so efficient, galactose 1-phosphate accumulates rapidly and is the main toxic mediator when GALT is deficient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galactokinase has a low, not high, Km; it works efficiently at low galactose concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high Km (low affinity) and NADPH use describe aldose reductase, not galactokinase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: UDP-glucose is the co-substrate of GALT, the second enzyme, not of galactokinase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactokinase has a high Vmax and uses ATP, not NADPH.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: In hepatocytes, galactose 1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) converts galactose 1-phosphate to glucose 1-phosphate. Which of the following correctly identifies the co-substrate consumed and the second product generated by the GALT reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP is consumed; ADP is produced

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose is consumed; lactose is produced

choices.label: C
choices.text: NADPH is consumed; NADP+ is produced

choices.label: D
choices.text: UDP-galactose is consumed; UDP-glucose is produced

choices.label: E
choices.text: UDP-glucose is consumed; UDP-galactose is produced

explanation.summary: GALT swaps the attached groups of galactose 1-phosphate and UDP-glucose, yielding glucose 1-phosphate and UDP-galactose.
explanation.whyCorrect: GALT converts galactose 1-phosphate to glucose 1-phosphate by switching the attached groups of galactose 1-phosphate and UDP-glucose. The reaction therefore consumes UDP-glucose and releases UDP-galactose, which GALE then reversibly isomerizes back to UDP-glucose so it can be used again in the pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP-to-ADP conversion occurs in the galactokinase step that precedes GALT, not in the GALT reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Combining glucose with UDP-galactose to make lactose is the lactose synthase reaction of mammary tissue, not GALT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NADPH consumption belongs to aldose reductase producing galactitol, not to GALT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the direction: GALT uses UDP-glucose and produces UDP-galactose; the reverse interconversion is the job of GALE.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant presents with jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, and hypoglycemia after breastfeeding. Testing reveals normal galactokinase and normal GALT activity, but a deficiency of UDP-galactose epimerase (GALE). Which of the following best explains why this rare form of galactosemia can be as severe as classical GALT deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galactose 1-phosphate can still be formed because the galactokinase step is intact

choices.label: B
choices.text: GALE deficiency completely blocks the phosphorylation of galactose by galactokinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: GALE deficiency prevents the formation of galactitol within the lens by aldose reductase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactase activity is secondarily lost from the intestinal brush border membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: UDP-glucose cannot be synthesized from glucose 1-phosphate in the liver

explanation.summary: Type III (GALE) galactosemia can match type I severity because the phosphorylated galactose, the main toxic mediator, can still be formed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type III galactosemia is a far rarer form caused by a lack of GALE, the enzyme that reversibly isomerizes UDP-galactose to UDP-glucose so it can be used again in the pathway. Its severity is similar to classic galactosemia because the phosphorylated galactose (galactose 1-phosphate) can still be formed by galactokinase, although select variants have a milder presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Galactokinase is intact in GALE deficiency, so galactose is still phosphorylated; this is precisely why the disease is severe.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GALE deficiency does not prevent galactitol formation; excess galactose is still available for aldose reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactase is not affected; galactose is still liberated from lactose and absorbed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The severity is explained by galactose 1-phosphate accumulation, not by an inability to make UDP-glucose from glucose 1-phosphate.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, dietary galactose is phosphorylated by galactokinase and then processed by GALT. The glucose-containing product of the GALT reaction can subsequently enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis. Which of the following is that product?

explanation.summary: GALT converts galactose 1-phosphate into glucose 1-phosphate, which feeds glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Galactokinase converts galactose to galactose 1-phosphate using ATP, and GALT then converts galactose 1-phosphate to glucose 1-phosphate by exchanging groups with UDP-glucose. Glucose 1-phosphate is the entry point of galactose carbon into glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galactitol is a dead-end product of aldose reductase formed only when galactose is in excess; it cannot be further metabolized.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Galactose 1-phosphate is the substrate of GALT, not the product that enters central metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactose is the dietary disaccharide source of galactose, not a product of the pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UDP-galactose is the other product of GALT, which GALE recycles to UDP-glucose; it does not directly enter glycolysis.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus develops bilateral cataracts. His ophthalmologist notes that the pathogenesis parallels the cataracts seen in infants with galactosemia. In this patient, excess glucose in the lens is converted to which of the following osmotically active compounds?

explanation.summary: In diabetes, excess glucose is converted to sorbitol in the lens, mirroring the galactose-to-galactitol process of galactosemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cataracts in galactosemia occur because excess galactose is converted to galactitol in the lens through aldose reductase, and galactitol build-up produces osmotic and oxidative stress that denatures and aggregates lens proteins. A similar process occurs with diabetes, in which excess glucose is converted to sorbitol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galactitol is the sugar alcohol derived from galactose in galactosemia, not from glucose in diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose 1-phosphate is a normal metabolic intermediate that enters glycolysis or gluconeogenesis; it is not the osmotic lens product.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen is a glucose storage polymer of liver and muscle and is not the cause of diabetic cataracts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactic acid is the osmotically active product of bacterial lactose fermentation in the gut, not a lens metabolite.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 5-day-old boy with undiagnosed classical galactosemia develops Escherichia coli sepsis. His pediatrician explains that the enzyme deficiency itself increases susceptibility to this infection. Which of the following best describes the cellular basis for this increased risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depletion of NADPH prevents antibody production by B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess galactose inside neutrophils impairs their bactericidal activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galactitol accumulation in hepatocytes reduces complement synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactic acid in the gut lumen promotes bacterial translocation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphate trapping in enterocytes disrupts the intestinal barrier

explanation.summary: In galactosemia, excess galactose within neutrophils impairs their bactericidal activity, putting newborns at risk for E. coli sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excess galactose inside neutrophils impairs their bactericidal activity, so newborns with galactosemia are at risk for Escherichia coli sepsis. This connection between galactose metabolism, immunology, and microbiology is an interdisciplinary point often tested on board exams.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NADPH consumption by aldose reductase lowers reduced glutathione and contributes to oxidative stress; it is not described as impairing antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sepsis risk is attributed to neutrophil dysfunction from galactose, not to reduced hepatic complement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Luminal lactic acid is the mechanism of diarrhea in lactose intolerance, not of sepsis in galactosemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphate trapping and ATP depletion impair hepatic gluconeogenesis and cause hypoglycemia; they are not the described cause of sepsis.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: Two exclusively breastfed newborns are evaluated. One has classical galactosemia and one has hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency). Both disorders involve ATP depletion and phosphate trapping in the liver, yet only the infant with galactosemia becomes symptomatic during the first days of life. Which of the following best explains this difference in timing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldolase B is not expressed until after weaning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Breast milk contains lactose but generally lacks fructose and sucrose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fructokinase is a low-efficiency enzyme, so fructose 1-phosphate accumulates only slowly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Galactose 1-phosphate is more toxic per molecule than fructose 1-phosphate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neonatal screening detects galactosemia but not fructose disorders

explanation.summary: Galactosemias present earlier than fructose disorders because breast milk supplies lactose (and thus galactose) but generally lacks fructose and sucrose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human breast milk generally lacks fructose and sucrose but contains lactose. This is why galactosemias typically present much earlier after birth than disorders in fructose metabolism: the toxic substrate for galactosemia is delivered with the very first feeds, whereas the fructose-intolerant infant is not exposed until fructose or sucrose enters the diet.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The timing difference is dietary exposure, not developmental expression of aldolase B.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fructokinase, much like galactokinase, is an extremely efficient enzyme that rapidly consumes ATP; the difference is substrate exposure, not enzyme speed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both disorders share a similar ATP depletion and phosphate trapping mechanism; relative toxicity per molecule is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Screening affects detection, not whether symptoms develop; the symptomatic difference reflects what the infant is fed.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with classical galactosemia, maintained on a strict lactose- and galactose-free diet since infancy, delivers a healthy infant and begins breastfeeding. Analysis of her breast milk shows normal lactose content. Which of the following best explains how her mammary glands produce lactose despite the absence of dietary galactose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldose reductase converts galactitol back into galactose for lactose synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galactokinase runs in reverse to release free galactose from galactose 1-phosphate

choices.label: C
choices.text: GALE converts UDP-glucose to UDP-galactose, which lactose synthase joins with glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactase in mammary tissue reassembles lactose from stored glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residual GALT activity in mammary tissue generates galactose 1-phosphate

explanation.summary: Mammary lactose synthase combines UDP-galactose and glucose, and UDP-galactose is supplied from UDP-glucose by the reversible GALE reaction, so dietary galactose is not required.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mammary glands express lactose synthase, which enzymatically converts UDP-galactose and glucose into the lactose disaccharide and free UDP. Because GALE interconverts UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose in both directions, individuals with galactosemia will still produce lactose in their milk despite limiting galactose in their diet. A lactating mother does not need to consume lactose or galactose for lactose to be produced in the milk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no enzyme that breaks down galactitol; it is a dead-end product and is not converted back to galactose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose using ATP; it is not the source of UDP-galactose for lactose synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactase cleaves lactose in the intestine; it is not the mammary enzyme that synthesizes lactose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GALT is the deficient enzyme in classical galactosemia, and its reaction does not generate the UDP-galactose needed for lactose synthesis from glucose.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 9-month-old girl who was healthy while exclusively breastfed develops vomiting, hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly shortly after fruit and sweetened foods are introduced into her diet. Her physician notes that the biochemical mechanism of her hypoglycemia, ATP depletion with phosphate trapping, is the same one seen in classical galactosemia. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this infant?

explanation.summary: Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) shares the ATP depletion and phosphate trapping mechanism of classical galactosemia but presents when fructose or sucrose enters the diet.
explanation.whyCorrect: A similar ATP depletion and phosphate trapping occurs in hereditary fructose intolerance, which is a deficiency of the enzyme aldolase B. Much like galactokinase, fructokinase is an extremely efficient enzyme that phosphorylates fructose by rapidly consuming ATP, so when the downstream enzyme aldolase B is deficient, phosphorylated fructose accumulates. Because breast milk generally lacks fructose and sucrose, symptoms appear only after these sugars are introduced.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fructokinase is the intact, highly efficient enzyme whose activity drives the phosphate trapping; its deficiency would prevent, not cause, the accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GALT deficiency is classical galactosemia, which presents in the first days of breastfeeding because breast milk contains lactose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Branching enzyme deficiency (Andersen disease) causes progressive liver cirrhosis from abnormally structured glycogen, not diet-triggered acute hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GALE deficiency (type III galactosemia) is triggered by galactose from lactose, not by the introduction of fruit.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A 4-day-old boy is flagged on newborn screening for classical galactosemia. He is currently exclusively breastfed and is not yet symptomatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate dietary intervention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue breastfeeding and add oral glucose supplements

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue breastfeeding with lactase enzyme drops added to each feed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restrict fructose and sucrose while continuing breast milk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to a lactose-free soy-based infant formula

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to a standard cow's-milk-based infant formula

explanation.summary: Infants with galactosemia should receive lactose-free soy-based formula, because a lactose- and galactose-free diet prevents all complications of the deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elimination of galactose-containing foods, primarily dairy products, is the mainstay of treatment for galactose metabolism disorders. Individuals with galactosemia should follow a strict diet such as drinking lactose-free soy-based infant formulas as infants. Most cases are now picked up by newborn screening, and proper dietary intervention implemented early prevents complications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast milk contains lactose and therefore galactose; adding glucose does nothing to remove the toxic substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactase drops would cleave lactose into glucose and galactose, still delivering galactose to an infant who cannot metabolize it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fructose and sucrose restriction is the strategy for hereditary fructose intolerance; breast milk lactose is the problem in galactosemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cow's-milk formula, like breast milk and most infant formulas, contains lactose and would continue galactose exposure.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: At a public hearing, a parent argues that galactokinase deficiency should be removed from the mandatory newborn screening panel because it is described as a mild condition. As a physician on the panel, which of the following is the most accurate argument for retaining it on the screen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affected infants develop Escherichia coli sepsis unless galactose is restricted at birth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess galactose forms galactitol in the lens, causing cataracts that early galactose elimination prevents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galactose 1-phosphate accumulates and causes hypoglycemia before symptoms are apparent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infants with the deficiency require lifelong enzyme replacement that must begin in infancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untreated galactokinase deficiency causes liver cirrhosis and intellectual disability within the first year

explanation.summary: Screening for galactokinase deficiency is justified because its main manifestation, cataracts from galactitol, is fully preventable by early dietary galactose elimination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Galactokinase deficiency is mild compared with classical galactosemia, but excess galactose still promotes galactitol formation in various tissues through aldose reductase, and the main clinical manifestation is cataracts, which usually present in childhood or young adulthood with early signs of visual impairment in infancy. A lactose- and galactose-free diet prevents all complications related to the enzyme deficiency, so identifying affected newborns before galactitol damages the lens is the rationale for screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli sepsis risk is described for the classical (type I) form with its systemic galactose toxicity, not as the argument for screening the mild type II form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galactokinase deficiency blocks the first step, so galactose 1-phosphate is never formed and hypoglycemia is not the concern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Treatment is dietary elimination of galactose-containing foods, not enzyme replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver dysfunction and mental disability are the severe features of classical galactosemia and are lacking in galactokinase deficiency.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I: Glycogen, Lactose Intolerance, and Galactosemia

questions.stem: A skeletal muscle cell accumulates high levels of glucose 6-phosphate during rest. Which enzyme's activity is most directly reduced as a consequence of this accumulation?

explanation.summary: Hexokinase is feedback-inhibited by its own product, glucose 6-phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hexokinase catalyzes step 1 of glycolysis and has a low Km and low Vmax. High glucose 6-phosphate signals that a cell's glucose/energy needs are met, so the product allosterically inhibits hexokinase to prevent trapping additional glucose that could be prioritized for other tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucokinase, the liver isozyme, is NOT inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate, allowing continued rapid glucose uptake when glucose is abundant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose 6-phosphatase is a gluconeogenic enzyme; its activity is not governed by product inhibition from glucose 6-phosphate in this manner.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PFK-1 is inhibited by ATP and citrate, not directly by glucose 6-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase (step 10) is inhibited by ATP, alanine, and glucagon signaling, not by glucose 6-phosphate.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A well-fed hepatocyte is exposed to high insulin during glucose abundance. Which molecule most directly increases glycolytic flux at phosphofructokinase-1?

explanation.summary: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is the potent allosteric activator of PFK-1 in the fed liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the liver, insulin promotes the kinase activity of the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2, which produces fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. This metabolite is a positive allosteric activator of PFK-1, speeding glycolysis so glucose can be used for glycogen replenishment and fatty acid synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alanine is an inhibitor of pyruvate kinase and a gluconeogenic substrate, not a PFK-1 activator.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ATP is a high-energy signal that inhibits PFK-1, slowing glycolysis when energy is abundant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Citrate, an early TCA intermediate, inhibits PFK-1 as a signal of sufficient biosynthetic and energy substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose 6-phosphate inhibits hexokinase (step 1) and is not the direct activator of PFK-1.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A fasting patient's hepatocytes are exposed to high glucagon, which raises intracellular cAMP and activates protein kinase A (PKA). Which of the following is most likely occurring in these liver cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate accumulates and promotes hepatic glycolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin activates the kinase domain of PFK-2, raising fructose 2,6-bisphosphate

choices.label: C
choices.text: PFK-1 is allosterically activated by fructose 2,6-bisphosphate to accelerate glycolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: PKA phosphorylates PFK-2, lowering fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and slowing glycolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate kinase is dephosphorylated and thereby activated

explanation.summary: Glucagon (via cAMP/PKA) phosphorylates PFK-2, activating its phosphatase function and lowering fructose 2,6-bisphosphate to slow hepatic glycolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: During fasting, glucagon binds hepatocytes, activating adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP, and activating PKA. PKA phosphorylates PFK-2, which suppresses its kinase activity and activates its FBPase-2 (phosphatase) activity. This decreases fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, reducing PFK-1 activation so the liver exports glucose rather than catabolizing it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is cleaved and decreases during fasting, slowing rather than promoting glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin (not glucagon) drives PFK-2 kinase activity; this state is dominated by glucagon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels fall in this state, so PFK-1 is not being activated by it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucagon/PKA phosphorylates and inhibits pyruvate kinase; it does not dephosphorylate/activate it.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, a hepatocyte converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate to sustain gluconeogenesis. Which enzyme catalyzes this step, requiring biotin and activation by acetyl-CoA?

explanation.summary: Pyruvate carboxylase adds CO2 to pyruvate to form oxaloacetate, requiring biotin (vitamin B7) and activation by acetyl-CoA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate carboxylase is a gluconeogenic bypass enzyme that carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate. It requires the cofactor biotin (vitamin B7) and is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA, which accumulates during fasting from fatty acid oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase cleaves a phosphate off fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, bypassing PFK-1, not the pyruvate step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose 6-phosphatase removes phosphate from glucose 6-phosphate for export; it does not act on pyruvate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PEPCK converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate; it acts after pyruvate carboxylase and does not use biotin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase runs the forward glycolytic step (PEP to pyruvate) and is not gluconeogenic.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A hepatocyte performs active gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis but is unable to release free glucose into the bloodstream via GLUT2. A deficiency of which enzyme best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Glucose 6-phosphatase removes the phosphate from glucose 6-phosphate so that glucose can be exported via GLUT2.
explanation.whyCorrect: There is no transporter for phosphorylated glucose. Glucose 6-phosphatase produces free glucose from glucose 6-phosphate, enabling export of glucose derived from both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Without it, the liver cannot release glucose to the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase acts at the fructose bisphosphate step, not the terminal glucose 6-phosphate step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose (traps it in the cell); its loss would not block export of already-formed glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PEPCK acts upstream converting oxaloacetate to PEP and does not dephosphorylate glucose 6-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate carboxylase forms oxaloacetate from pyruvate, an early gluconeogenic step, not the final export step.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: An investigational drug inhibits the malate-aspartate shuttle in hepatocytes. Which of the following is most likely to increase as a direct result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA cycle

explanation.summary: Blocking NADH shuttles causes cytosolic NADH to accumulate, driving pyruvate toward lactate.
explanation.whyCorrect: There is no mitochondrial NAD+/NADH transporter, so cytosolic NADH from glycolysis reaches the ETC only through shuttles. Inhibiting the malate-aspartate shuttle leaves cytosolic NADH elevated, shifting the lactate dehydrogenase equilibrium to convert pyruvate to lactate and regenerate NAD+.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA is not increased; impaired NADH transfer reduces overall oxidative flux.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gluconeogenesis would fall, since accumulated NADH diverts pyruvate to lactate rather than to glucose synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ATP yield would decrease because glycolytic reducing equivalents no longer reach the ETC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidative phosphorylation would decrease because fewer reducing equivalents reach the electron transport chain.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: Mature red blood cells lack mitochondria and rely entirely on glycolysis for ATP. Which fate of pyruvate allows these cells to regenerate NAD+ and sustain glycolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carboxylation to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduction to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase

explanation.summary: In RBCs, pyruvate is reduced to lactate by LDH, regenerating NAD+ needed to keep glycolysis running.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because RBCs cannot oxidize NADH in mitochondria, they must regenerate cytosolic NAD+ another way. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD+, allowing glycolysis (the RBC's only ATP source) to continue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyruvate carboxylase is mitochondrial and gluconeogenic; RBCs do not perform this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PDH requires mitochondria, which mature RBCs lack, so acetyl-CoA formation cannot occur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RBCs do not perform gluconeogenesis; that is a hepatic (and renal) process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alanine formation via ALT does not regenerate NAD+ and is not the RBC's mechanism for sustaining glycolysis.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate, generating NADH and CO2. Which of its required coenzymes is derived from niacin (vitamin B3)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coenzyme A (CoA), the acyl group carrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), the E3 cofactor

explanation.summary: NAD+ is the PDH coenzyme derived from niacin (vitamin B3).
explanation.whyCorrect: The PDH complex requires five coenzymes. NAD+, derived from niacin (vitamin B3), is the terminal electron acceptor that is reduced to NADH during the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coenzyme A is derived from pantothenate (vitamin B5).
whyWrongByChoice.B: FAD is derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoate is derived from octanoic acid, a fatty acid, not from niacin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP) is derived from thiamin (vitamin B1), not niacin.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with two months of fatigue, difficulty walking, and new peripheral pain. Five months ago he began eating mostly white rice after losing his job. Exam shows pronounced calf muscle weakness; labs reveal a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate. Which enzyme is most likely adversely affected?

explanation.summary: A white-rice diet causes thiamin deficiency, which compromises the thiamin (TPP)-dependent pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PDH complex requires thiamin (as TPP), which becomes deficient with a polished-rice diet. Impaired PDH activity causes pyruvate to accumulate and shift toward lactate (lactic/metabolic acidosis) and greatly limits ATP production, accounting for the weakness. This is the beriberi picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase requires niacin-derived NADP+, not thiamin, and its deficiency causes hemolysis, not this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PFK-1 is a glycolytic control point enzyme that does not require a vitamin-derived coenzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PFK-2 regulates fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and does not require a thiamin coenzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme not dependent on a vitamin-derived coenzyme.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A patient with severe thiamin deficiency presents with lower extremity edema and dilated cardiomyopathy. Which classification best describes this presentation?

explanation.summary: Wet beriberi is the cardiovascular form of thiamin deficiency, with edema and dilated cardiomyopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beriberi has two classifications by presentation: wet beriberi is cardiovascular in nature, presenting with edema due to dilated cardiomyopathy, whereas dry beriberi is neuromuscular. This patient's edema and dilated cardiomyopathy define the wet form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dry beriberi is neuromuscular, presenting with muscle weakness and peripheral nerve pain (typically in the legs), not cardiac edema.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Korsakoff dementia is a chronic amnestic syndrome with confabulation, not a cardiovascular presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pellagra results from niacin (B3) deficiency, causing dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wernicke encephalopathy presents with ataxia, confusion, and ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, not dilated cardiomyopathy.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A disoriented patient with a history of chronic alcohol abuse is hypoglycemic and acidotic. The attending insists on giving thiamin before administering IV dextrose. What is the best rationale for giving thiamin first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dextrose directly inhibits transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dextrose precipitates hemolysis in thiamin-deficient patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose administration acutely raises blood ammonia levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamin is required to activate glucokinase before glucose can be phosphorylated

explanation.summary: In thiamin deficiency, PDH cannot fully oxidize administered glucose, so giving dextrose before thiamin can be harmful.
explanation.whyCorrect: PDH requires thiamin (TPP). If a chronically malnourished alcoholic is thiamin-deficient, administered glucose cannot be properly oxidized through PDH, and the glucose load can precipitate or worsen thiamin-dependent enzyme failure, driving lactic acidosis and neurologic decline (e.g., Wernicke encephalopathy). A thiamin bolus should ensure PDH is functional before glucose is given.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dextrose does not directly inhibit transketolase; the problem is a lack of thiamin cofactor, not glucose-mediated inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dextrose does not cause hemolysis in thiamin deficiency; the risk is metabolic and neurologic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The danger relates to impaired glucose oxidation, not an acute rise in ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucokinase does not require thiamin; the thiamin-dependent enzyme in glucose oxidation is PDH.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A patient has chronic hemolytic anemia, and a peripheral smear shows echinocytes (burr cells) with evenly distributed spiky surfaces. Deficiency of which glycolytic enzyme in red blood cells best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: RBC pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolytic anemia with echinocytes (burr cells).
explanation.whyCorrect: RBCs depend entirely on glycolysis for ATP. Pyruvate kinase deficiency depletes ATP; without ATP, Na/K pumps fail and the membrane retracts, producing echinocytes (burr cells) with evenly distributed spiky surfaces and chronic hemolytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells, not echinocytes from ATP depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hexokinase deficiency is not the enzyme specifically linked in this brick to hemolysis with echinocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate dehydrogenase deficiency does not produce this classic ATP-depletion echinocyte picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PFK-1 deficiency is not the cause described here; the brick attributes RBC hemolysis and burr cells to pyruvate kinase.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A single molecule of glucose is converted to pyruvate by glycolysis in a hepatocyte. Accounting for both the investment and production phases, which of the following best describes the net yield of this pathway?

explanation.summary: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP, 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate per glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Much like a monetary investment, 2 ATP are spent in the investment phase of glycolysis and 4 ATP are made in the production phase, for a net of 2 ATP. The production phase also generates 2 NADH (reducing power for the ETC/OXPHOS), and the six-carbon hexose is split into two three-carbon pyruvates that can produce acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycolysis generates NADH, not FADH2; FADH2 arises in the glycerol-phosphate shuttle, not in glycolysis itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycolysis produces 2 NADH, not 4, and two pyruvates rather than one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 4 ATP is the gross production; 2 ATP were invested initially, so the net is only 2 ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both the ATP and NADH figures are overstated; net ATP is 2 and NADH is 2.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A hepatocyte metabolizes dietary galactose. Galactose is ultimately converted to which of the following molecules in order to feed back into glycolysis?

explanation.summary: Galactose is ultimately converted to glucose 1-phosphate, which feeds back into glycolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycolysis is the central pathway of carbohydrate metabolism because nearly all sugars feed into it. Galactose is ultimately converted to glucose 1-phosphate, which then feeds back into glycolysis. By contrast, fructose metabolism starts very distinct from glycolysis before converging into the pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate is a glycolytic intermediate used in the glycerol-phosphate shuttle, not the product of galactose conversion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is the product of the PFK-1 committed step, not the galactose entry point.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fructose 6-phosphate is the substrate of PFK-1 in glycolysis, not the entry product of galactose metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphoenolpyruvate is the substrate of pyruvate kinase at step 10, far downstream of where galactose enters.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, portal glucose rises sharply and hepatocytes rapidly phosphorylate glucose to maximize storage via glycogenesis and lipid synthesis. Which set of properties of the hepatic isozyme responsible for this step best explains this behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High Km, high Vmax, not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate

choices.label: B
choices.text: High Km, low Vmax, not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low Km, high Vmax, inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low Km, high Vmax, not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low Km, low Vmax, inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate

explanation.summary: Glucokinase has a high Km (low affinity) and very high Vmax and is not product-inhibited, so it rapidly converts glucose whenever glucose is abundant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucokinase, the liver isozyme, has low affinity (high Km) for glucose but a very high Vmax. It binds and metabolizes glucose only at high concentrations, but once active the conversion is rapid. Unlike hexokinase, glucokinase is not inhibited by its product, glucose 6-phosphate, allowing continued rapid conversion as long as glucose levels are high to maximize storage via glycogenesis and lipid synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucokinase has a very high Vmax, not a low one; a low Vmax would prevent the rapid conversion seen in the fed liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucokinase has a high Km (low affinity), and it is specifically not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucokinase has low affinity (high Km) for glucose, so it is only active at high glucose concentrations, not low ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Low Km, low Vmax, and product inhibition describe hexokinase, the isozyme in tissues with limited glucose utilization capacity.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: Most reactions of glycolysis are readily reversible and run in reverse during gluconeogenesis. Which of the following correctly pairs the number of irreversible glycolytic control points with the number of unique enzymes gluconeogenesis uses to bypass them?

explanation.summary: Glycolysis has three irreversible control points (steps 1, 3, and 10), which gluconeogenesis bypasses with four unique enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Steps 1, 3, and 10 of glycolysis are the three irreversible, heavily regulated control points. Gluconeogenesis uses four enzymes to bypass them: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase together reverse step 10, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses step 3, and glucose 6-phosphatase bypasses step 1. All other steps are shared between the two pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There are three control points, not two, and four bypass enzymes are needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The number of unique enzymes (four) is correct, but there are three control points, not two.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although there are three control points, step 10 requires two enzymes (pyruvate carboxylase and PEPCK) to reverse, giving four unique enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only steps 1, 3, and 10 are irreversible control points; there are three, not four.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A hepatocyte diverts glucose-derived intermediates into the pentose phosphate pathway. Which of the following best explains why intermediates can be diverted into other pathways before step 3 of glycolysis but not after it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate inhibits the pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hexokinase catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: PFK-1 catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyruvate kinase is the only irreversible glycolytic step

choices.label: E
choices.text: Steps after PFK-1 are freely reversible

explanation.summary: PFK-1 catalyzes the committed step: intermediates before it can feed other pathways, but after it pyruvate production is guaranteed.
explanation.whyCorrect: PFK-1, the most heavily regulated glycolytic enzyme, converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. This step is dubbed the committed step because intermediates feed other pathways (e.g., the pentose phosphate pathway) preceding it, but after this step pyruvate production is guaranteed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes no inhibition of the pentose phosphate pathway by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate; diversion is prevented because the committed step has been passed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hexokinase catalyzes step 1, which is irreversible but not the committed step; its product glucose 6-phosphate can still be diverted to other pathways.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Steps 1, 3, and 10 are all irreversible; pyruvate kinase is not the only irreversible step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversibility of later steps is not the reason; the committed nature of PFK-1 is what guarantees pyruvate production afterward.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: During a sprint, skeletal muscle rapidly consumes ATP. Which of the following changes most directly increases the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 in this muscle?

explanation.summary: AMP is the low-energy signal that activates PFK-1, favoring glycolysis when cellular energy is low.
explanation.whyCorrect: When cellular energy is low, PFK-1 is activated and glycolysis is favored. AMP is the low-energy signal that activates PFK-1. In contracting muscle that is consuming ATP, rising AMP directly increases PFK-1 activity to accelerate glycolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alanine is an inhibitor of pyruvate kinase in the liver, not a regulator of PFK-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ATP is a high-energy signal that inhibits PFK-1; it falls, rather than rises, in a sprinting muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Citrate, an early intermediate of the TCA cycle, is a high-energy signal that inhibits PFK-1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose 6-phosphate inhibits hexokinase at step 1; it is not an activator of PFK-1.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A newly characterized hepatic enzyme is shown to be anabolic and to be a substrate of protein kinase A (PKA). Based on the general rules of hormonal regulation of metabolic enzymes, which of the following is the most likely effect of glucagon on this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation via a decrease in intracellular cAMP

explanation.summary: Glucagon phosphorylates enzymes via PKA, and phosphorylating anabolic enzymes is inhibitory.
explanation.whyCorrect: As a rule of thumb, glucagon tends to phosphorylate metabolic enzymes via the action of PKA, whereas insulin culminates in the activity of a central phosphatase that dephosphorylates enzymes. Because insulin is anabolic, dephosphorylation of anabolic enzymes activates them; the opposite is true for glucagon, so phosphorylating anabolic enzymes is inhibitory while phosphorylating catabolic enzymes promotes activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucagon increases cAMP through adenylate cyclase; a decrease in cAMP is the effect of insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dephosphorylation of anabolic enzymes is activating, but that is the insulin (phosphatase) pathway, not glucagon's action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PKA phosphorylation activates catabolic enzymes, but for an anabolic enzyme phosphorylation is inhibitory.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucagon acts through phosphorylation, not dephosphorylation, and dephosphorylation of an anabolic enzyme would activate rather than inhibit it.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: During an overnight fast, hepatic pyruvate kinase activity is suppressed by ATP. Which of the following best characterizes the source and nature of this inhibitory ATP signal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bodily ATP abundance reflecting the fed state

choices.label: B
choices.text: A localized cellular ATP rise from fatty acid oxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: ATP generated by hepatic glycolysis of dietary glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: ATP imported from the circulation through GLUT2

choices.label: E
choices.text: ATP released during hepatic glycogen breakdown

explanation.summary: In fasting, fatty acid oxidation raises ATP locally within hepatocytes to fuel gluconeogenesis, and this localized ATP inhibits pyruvate kinase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Energy levels rise in the liver during fasting because fatty acid oxidation provides ample ATP to fuel gluconeogenesis. This is a localized cellular ATP increase within the hepatocyte, not to be confused with a bodily ATP abundance. That ATP inhibits pyruvate kinase so hepatic glycolysis is suppressed while glucose is produced and exported.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick stresses this is a localized cellular ATP increase, not to be confused with a bodily ATP abundance; the body is in a fasting, not fed, state.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic glycolysis is inhibited during fasting; the ATP comes from fatty acid oxidation, not glycolysis of dietary glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT2 transports glucose, not ATP; there is no import of ATP from the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogen breakdown supplies glucose for export; the ATP that inhibits pyruvate kinase is derived from fatty acid oxidation.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, glucagon signaling increases the hepatic abundance of an amino acid that alanine aminotransferase (ALT) converts to pyruvate in a single step to supply gluconeogenesis. Which additional effect does this amino acid exert on hepatic glycolysis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activation of the kinase function of PFK-2

explanation.summary: Alanine, which becomes more abundant with glucagon, is converted to pyruvate by ALT and also inhibits hepatic pyruvate kinase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alanine is one of the signals that suppresses pyruvate kinase during low blood glucose. Through a one-step conversion via ALT, alanine becomes pyruvate to provide substrate for gluconeogenesis, and alanine becomes more abundant when glucagon is present. Inhibiting pyruvate kinase prevents that pyruvate-bound carbon from being re-consumed by glycolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hexokinase is regulated by glucose 6-phosphate inhibition, not by alanine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PFK-1 is activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; alanine is not a PFK-1 activator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kinase function of PFK-2 is promoted by insulin during glucose abundance, not by alanine in fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose 6-phosphatase is needed to export glucose during fasting; alanine does not inhibit it.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: Which of the following molecules activates hepatic pyruvate kinase through a feed-forward mechanism?

explanation.summary: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, the product of PFK-1, feeds forward to activate pyruvate kinase in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate kinase within the liver is activated by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate in a feed-forward mechanism. Once PFK-1 has committed intermediates to glycolysis by producing fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, that product signals downstream to pyruvate kinase to complete the pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase, a gluconeogenic enzyme, not pyruvate kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Citrate is a high-energy signal that inhibits PFK-1; it is not a pyruvate kinase activator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is the PFK-2 product that allosterically activates PFK-1, not pyruvate kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose 6-phosphate is a feedback inhibitor of hexokinase and does not activate pyruvate kinase.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A patient in the third week of starvation has sustained hepatic gluconeogenesis. Oxaloacetate produced in the TCA cycle is being diverted to sustain glucose synthesis. Which of the following is the most direct metabolic consequence of this diversion within the liver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased acetyl-CoA oxidation in the TCA cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased net conversion of acetyl-CoA to glucose

explanation.summary: Siphoning oxaloacetate from the TCA cycle for gluconeogenesis slows the hepatic TCA cycle, contributing to ketone body formation in prolonged fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because oxaloacetate is also produced in the TCA cycle, mechanisms exist to divert or siphon OAA in times of great need from the TCA to sustain gluconeogenesis. The tradeoff is slowing of the TCA within the liver, which is a factor that contributes to ketone body formation during long-term fasting or starvation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diverting oxaloacetate slows the TCA cycle, so acetyl-CoA oxidation decreases rather than increases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic glycolysis is inhibited during fasting so that glucose is exported rather than oxidized.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetyl-CoA can never be used for the net synthesis of glucose, regardless of oxaloacetate availability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase is suppressed in the fasting liver by glucagon signaling, ATP, and alanine.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: Several molecules can supply carbon to hepatic gluconeogenesis during fasting. Which of the following can never be used for the net synthesis of glucose?

explanation.summary: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase but can never serve as a substrate for net glucose synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alanine, lactate, and a variety of other molecules produce pyruvate to supply gluconeogenesis with substrate. However, acetyl-CoA can never be used for the net synthesis of glucose. Its role in gluconeogenesis is regulatory, as an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, not as a carbon source.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alanine is converted to pyruvate in one step by ALT and is a substrate for gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate produces pyruvate to supply gluconeogenesis with substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxaloacetate is converted by PEPCK to phosphoenolpyruvate and is a direct gluconeogenic intermediate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate is carboxylated by pyruvate carboxylase to oxaloacetate and is the entry substrate for gluconeogenesis.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: In a fasting hepatocyte with low glucose, glucokinase is found in an inactive complex with a regulatory protein within the nucleus. Which of the following best describes the purpose of this arrangement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allows glucokinase to phosphorylate glucose within the nucleus while fasting continues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Converts glucokinase into the hexokinase isozyme during periods of fasting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keeps a protected reserve of glucokinase inactive while gluconeogenesis proceeds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marks glucokinase for degradation by cytoplasmic proteases during fasting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Permanently inactivates glucokinase until the next meal has been absorbed

explanation.summary: Glucokinase-regulatory protein (GKRP) sequesters an inactive, protease-protected reserve of glucokinase in the nucleus so glycolysis does not compete with gluconeogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: GKRP maintains an inactive reserve of glucokinase within the nucleus. Sequestering glucokinase there prevents its glycolytic activity in the cytoplasm and protects it from degradation by cytoplasmic proteases. When glucose is low, glucokinase-GKRP complexes are held in the nucleus, favoring gluconeogenesis; these reserves are rapidly made available in response to rising glucose, the regulatory molecule for glucokinase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nuclear complex is inactive; glucokinase's glycolytic activity occurs in the cytoplasm once it is released.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucokinase and hexokinase are distinct isozymes; one is not converted into the other.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear sequestration protects glucokinase from cytoplasmic proteases rather than targeting it for degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reserve is rapidly made available in response to increasing glucose, so the inactivation is reversible, not permanent.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: Cytosolic NADH generated during glycolysis must deliver its reducing equivalents to the mitochondrial electron transport chain to maximize energy yield from glucose. Which of the following best explains why shuttle systems are required for this transfer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycolytic NADH is consumed by lactate dehydrogenase in all tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: NAD+ is synthesized only within the mitochondrial matrix

choices.label: C
choices.text: NADH is degraded in the cytosol before reaching the mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electron transport chain accepts electrons only from FADH2

choices.label: E
choices.text: There are no known NAD+/NADH transporters in the mitochondria

explanation.summary: Because mitochondria lack NAD+/NADH transporters, shuttles convert the reduction potential of cytosolic NADH into a molecule that does have a mitochondrial transporter.
explanation.whyCorrect: To date, there are no known NAD+/NADH transporters in the mitochondria. Yet NADH reducing equivalents from glycolysis are transferred to the ETC by two shuttle systems (malate-aspartate and glycerol-phosphate). The general strategy is to transform the reduction potential of glycolytic NADH into a molecule for which a mitochondrial transporter exists.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactate dehydrogenase consumes NADH in RBCs and in tissues lacking oxygen, not in all tissues; the shuttles exist for aerobic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NAD+ is present in both cytosol and matrix; the issue is transport, not the site of synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NADH is not degraded; it is reoxidized by the shuttle, transferring its electrons to a transportable carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ETC accepts electrons from NADH within the matrix; the problem is getting cytosolic reducing equivalents across the membrane.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: In the glycerol-phosphate shuttle, cytosolic NADH reduces dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glycerol 3-phosphate. When the mitochondrial glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase in the inner mitochondrial membrane reoxidizes this carrier, which molecule directly receives the electrons?

explanation.summary: The mitochondrial glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase passes electrons from glycerol 3-phosphate to FAD, forming FADH2 for the ETC.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the glycerol-phosphate shuttle, cytosolic NADH is used by cytosolic glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase to reduce DHAP, a glycolytic intermediate, to glycerol 3-phosphate. This reduced carrier passes its electrons onto FAD to form FADH2 within the mitochondrial membrane, which then feeds the electron transport chain. The enzyme reaction is reversible and exists in cytosolic and mitochondrial forms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coenzyme A is a PDH coenzyme that carries acyl groups, not electrons from glycerol 3-phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malate is the carrier in the malate-aspartate shuttle; it is not an electron acceptor in the glycerol-phosphate shuttle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAD+ is the acceptor in the cytosolic half of the reaction (regenerating NADH is not the goal); the mitochondrial enzyme uses FAD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxaloacetate is part of the malate-aspartate shuttle, not the glycerol-phosphate shuttle.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A neuron with functional mitochondria and adequate oxygen converts glucose to pyruvate via glycolysis. Which of the following is the most likely immediate fate of this pyruvate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidation to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduction to lactate for NAD+ regeneration

explanation.summary: In skeletal muscle and CNS tissue with sufficient oxygen and functional mitochondria, pyruvate is converted by PDH to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the TCA cycle for ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: During times of activity, metabolically active tissues such as skeletal muscle and the CNS convert glucose to pyruvate via glycolysis. If oxygen is sufficient and mitochondria are functional, this pyruvate is converted by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex to acetyl-CoA, which is subsequently oxidized within the TCA cycle to yield ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carboxylation to oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis is a hepatic fate during fasting, not a neuronal fate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis is the fed-state hepatic fate of pyruvate, not the neuron's use of glucose for energy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactate production is the fate in RBCs, or in other tissues when oxygen is insufficient or flux creates excess pyruvate; this neuron has adequate oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alanine production from pyruvate occurs in the liver in times of abundance via reversible ALT; it does not fuel gluconeogenesis in a neuron.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires five distinct coenzymes. Which of these coenzymes is derived from a fatty acid rather than from a vitamin?

explanation.summary: Lipoate (lipoamide) is derived from octanoic acid, a fatty acid, whereas the other four PDH coenzymes derive from B vitamins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the five PDH coenzymes, four are vitamin-derived: TPP from thiamin (B1), FAD from riboflavin (B2), NAD+ from niacin (B3), and CoA from pantothenate (B5). Lipoate (lipoamide) is the exception; its parent molecule is octanoic acid, a fatty acid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coenzyme A is derived from pantothenate (vitamin B5).
whyWrongByChoice.B: FAD is derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2).
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAD+ is derived from niacin (vitamin B3).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamin pyrophosphate is derived from thiamin (vitamin B1).

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: In a resting hepatocyte with abundant NADH and acetyl-CoA, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is found predominantly in a phosphorylated state. Which of the following best describes the regulatory mechanism responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PDH kinase is inhibited by acetyl-CoA and activates the complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: PDH kinase is stimulated by NADH and acetyl-CoA and inactivates the complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: PDH kinase is stimulated by pyruvate and inactivates the complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: PDH phosphatase is inhibited by ADP and inactivates the complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: PDH phosphatase is stimulated by NADH and inactivates the complex

explanation.summary: High-energy signals (NADH, acetyl-CoA) stimulate the PDH kinase subunit, which phosphorylates and inactivates the PDH complex.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PDH complex has its own kinase and phosphatase subunits that auto-regulate it via post-translational modification. When energy is high (abundant NADH and acetyl-CoA), the kinase phosphorylates and inactivates the PDH complex. This same inhibitory kinase is itself inhibited when low-energy signals such as ADP and pyruvate predominate, so that PDH is highly active when energy is low or being rapidly consumed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA activates (not inhibits) the kinase, and kinase activity inactivates the complex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyruvate, a low-energy substrate signal, inhibits the kinase rather than stimulating it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ADP inhibits the kinase, not the phosphatase; and the phosphatase activates rather than inactivates PDH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The phosphatase dephosphorylates and activates PDH, and it is stimulated by calcium, not NADH.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: During sustained skeletal muscle contraction, intracellular calcium is released and ATP is consumed. Which of the following effects on the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex results most directly from the rise in calcium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct allosteric inhibition of the complex by calcium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased conversion of thiamin to thiamin pyrophosphate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stimulation of the kinase subunit, inactivating the complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of the phosphatase subunit, activating the complex

explanation.summary: Calcium stimulates the PDH phosphatase, which dephosphorylates and activates PDH; this is a muscle-specific regulation tied to contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PDH phosphatase is stimulated by intracellular calcium to activate PDH activity. This is typically a muscle-specific regulation, because calcium is released during muscle contraction, which consumes ATP. Activating PDH under these conditions increases acetyl-CoA supply to the TCA cycle to aid ATP production when energy is being rapidly consumed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium acts through the phosphatase subunit, not as a direct allosteric inhibitor of the complex.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NADH product inhibition is unrelated to calcium and would decrease, not increase, PDH activity during ATP consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium does not regulate the conversion of thiamin to TPP; the coenzyme requirement is independent of contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The kinase is stimulated by high-energy signals (NADH, acetyl-CoA), not by calcium, and its action would be counterproductive in contracting muscle.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A patient with severe thiamin deficiency has metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate. In addition to pyruvate, an α-keto acid intermediate of the TCA cycle is accumulating because its TPP-dependent dehydrogenase is impaired. Which of the following TCA cycle enzymes is most directly impaired in this patient?

explanation.summary: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase requires TPP; thiamin deficiency causes α-ketoglutarate to accumulate, contributing to metabolic acidosis and disrupting the TCA cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thiamin (as TPP) is required for oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids. α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase converts α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA in the TCA cycle. Thiamin deficiency results in accumulation of α-ketoglutarate, an α-keto acid that contributes to metabolic acidosis, and energy production is further limited as the TCA is disrupted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrate synthase does not require TPP, and citrate is not an α-keto acid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is not TPP-dependent; the brick identifies α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase as the thiamin-dependent TCA enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malate dehydrogenase does not require TPP, and malate is not an α-keto acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Succinate dehydrogenase is not a TPP-dependent enzyme, and its substrate succinate is not an α-keto acid.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A patient with chronic thiamin deficiency reports profound muscle weakness even at rest. Thiamin deficiency blunts energy production from which of the following sources, which normally supplies about 20% of ATP in resting skeletal muscle?

explanation.summary: The TPP-dependent α-ketoacid dehydrogenase is required for oxidative catabolism of branched-chain amino acids, which supply about 20% of ATP in resting muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: α-Ketoacid dehydrogenase, a TPP-dependent enzyme, is required for the oxidative catabolism of branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) for energy production; roughly 20% of ATP in resting muscle derives from BCAA. Thiamin deficiency blunts energy production from BCAA oxidation, and accumulation of the BCAA α-keto acid intermediates potentiates metabolic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Creatine phosphate is not an oxidative source described in this brick and does not require thiamin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ketone bodies fuel the nervous system in prolonged starvation and are not the thiamin-dependent 20% ATP source in resting muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fatty acid oxidation does not depend on a TPP-requiring α-keto acid dehydrogenase and is not the source the brick attributes to 20% of resting muscle ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogenolysis supplies glucose for glycolysis; the thiamin-dependent step affecting muscle here is BCAA catabolism.

questions.topicName: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview II

questions.stem: A clinician wants a classic laboratory diagnostic for thiamin deficiency rather than relying on the patient's clinical presentation. Measurement of the activity of which of the following TPP-dependent enzymes is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Transketolase, the TPP-dependent enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway, is the classic diagnostic for thiamin deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transketolase is required for the pentose phosphate pathway and requires TPP. While the other thiamin-dependent enzymes (PDH, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, α-ketoacid dehydrogenase) have a prominent patient-presentation component, transketolase is the classic diagnostic for thiamin deficiency.
