As soon as glucose is re-introduced the brain abruptly switches to carbohydrate catabolism, and ketone body production ceases nearly immediately within the liver due to hormonal changes. This asymmetry in timing is clinically important.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ketogenesis ceases nearly immediately because of hormonal changes, not after slow enzyme degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cells lack mitochondria and can never consume ketone bodies; they use glucose exclusively.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The adaptation to ketone bodies is slow, but the return to glucose is abrupt, not delayed by days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The liver expresses only nominal beta-ketoacyl-CoA transferase and does not consume ketone bodies under any dietary state.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and poor nutrition has not eaten for several days and is found obtunded and hypoglycemic. Thiamin is administered before intravenous glucose. Which of the following best explains the rationale for this sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The brain needs thiamin to use glucose, and glucose halts ketone production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thiamin is a required cofactor for beta-ketoacyl-CoA transferase in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thiamin is required for hepatic HMG-CoA synthase activity during fasting

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thiamin itself serves as an alternative oxidizable fuel for the CNS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamin raises the NADH:NAD+ ratio to favor hepatic gluconeogenesis

explanation.summary: Giving glucose shuts off ketogenesis; if a thiamin-deficient brain cannot use that glucose, the CNS is left with no energy source.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once glucose is re-introduced, hepatic ketone body production ceases nearly immediately due to hormonal changes. If the brain is unable to utilize the provided glucose after prolonged deprivation due to compounding vitamin deficiencies, notably thiamin, there is no longer any alternative energy source for the CNS, leading to dire consequences. This is why thiamin is administered before or along with glucose in hypoglycemic chronic alcoholics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: beta-Ketoacyl-CoA transferase activates acetoacetate in ketolysis; thiamin's importance here is for glucose use by the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HMG-CoA synthase is a hepatic ketogenic enzyme; thiamin is emphasized for CNS glucose utilization, not for ketone synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thiamin is a vitamin required for glucose utilization, not a fuel that can be oxidized for CNS energy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rising NADH:NAD+ ratio from alcohol metabolism impairs gluconeogenesis; thiamin is not given to raise it.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: During a prolonged fast, hepatic acetyl-CoA rises markedly as beta-oxidation outpaces the TCA cycle. In addition to promoting ketone body formation, what effect does this accumulating acetyl-CoA have on the enzymes governing the fate of pyruvate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activates both the PDH complex and pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activates the PDH complex and inhibits pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits both the PDH complex and pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits pyruvate carboxylase with no effect on the PDH complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits the PDH complex and activates pyruvate carboxylase

explanation.summary: Accumulating acetyl-CoA inhibits the PDH complex and activates pyruvate carboxylase, driving gluconeogenesis alongside ketogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The accumulation of acetyl-CoA that promotes ketone body formation concomitantly drives gluconeogenesis by inhibiting the PDH complex and activating pyruvate carboxylase. Pyruvate is thus diverted away from oxidation and toward oxaloacetate and glucose production, coordinating the fasting response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA does not activate the PDH complex; it inhibits it while activating pyruvate carboxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the reverse of the true regulation; acetyl-CoA inhibits, rather than activates, the PDH complex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyruvate carboxylase is activated, not inhibited, by acetyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase and does inhibit the PDH complex.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: Ketone body synthesis in the mitochondrial matrix requires four enzymatic activities. Which of these is expressed in appreciable amounts only within the liver, thereby restricting ketogenesis to that organ?

explanation.summary: HMG-CoA synthase, which irreversibly forms HMG-CoA, is only expressed in appreciable amounts in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The second step of ketogenesis is the irreversible formation of HMG-CoA through the addition of another acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA via HMG-CoA synthase. This enzyme is only expressed in appreciable amounts within the liver, which is why the liver is the site of ketone body synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase is expressed in the liver and in tissues that consume ketone bodies to interconvert acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: beta-Ketoacyl-CoA transferase is a ketolysis enzyme that is expressed only nominally in the liver, the opposite pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HMG-CoA lyase catalyzes the irreversible cleavage to acetoacetate but is not the enzyme described as liver-restricted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiolase is widely expressed; it is the terminal enzyme of beta-oxidation and functions in both ketone synthesis and ketolysis.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: The first step of ketone body synthesis is the reversible condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules to form acetoacetyl-CoA. The enzyme catalyzing this step also participates in another pathway. Which reaction does the same enzyme catalyze?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The activation of acetoacetate in ketone-consuming tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: The carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reduction of HMG-CoA to mevalonate

choices.label: E
choices.text: The very last step of beta-oxidation of fatty acids

explanation.summary: Thiolase forms acetoacetyl-CoA in ketogenesis and is the same enzyme used in the very last step of beta-oxidation.
explanation.whyCorrect: For synthesis, the first step involves reversible formation of acetoacetyl-CoA by thiolase, which uses two acetyl-CoA molecules. This is the same enzyme used in the very last step of beta-oxidation. Because thiolase is reversible, it is also one of the enzymes of ketone body utilization, cleaving acetoacetyl-CoA back into acetyl-CoA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetoacetate is activated to acetoacetyl-CoA by beta-ketoacyl-CoA transferase, not by thiolase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate carboxylation to oxaloacetate is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase, a gluconeogenic enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis is catalyzed by HMG-CoA reductase, not thiolase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The reduction of HMG-CoA to mevalonate is the HMG-CoA reductase reaction of cholesterol synthesis.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: In skeletal muscle during fasting, acetoacetate is converted to acetoacetyl-CoA by beta-ketoacyl-CoA transferase so that its carbons can enter the TCA cycle. Which molecule donates the coenzyme A in this transferase reaction?

explanation.summary: beta-Ketoacyl-CoA transferase transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA (from the TCA cycle) to acetoacetate, releasing succinate back to the TCA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ketolysis produces acetyl-CoA from ketone bodies using beta-ketoacyl-CoA transferase, which converts acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA. In this reaction succinyl-CoA drawn from the TCA cycle donates its CoA and is released as succinate, which returns to the TCA. This step circumvents the irreversible synthesis reactions (HMG-CoA synthase and lyase) so that the packaged acetyl-CoA can be extracted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA is the final product of ketolysis released by thiolase, not the CoA donor for activating acetoacetate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HMG-CoA is an intermediate of the irreversible synthesis steps that ketolysis bypasses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malonyl-CoA is not part of the ketolysis pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Palmitoyl-CoA is a fatty acyl-CoA for beta-oxidation, not the CoA donor in ketolysis.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes who adheres strictly to her insulin regimen develops diabetic ketoacidosis during an episode of pneumonia. Which of the following best explains why an infection can precipitate DKA despite appropriate insulin dosing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial toxins directly destroy the remaining insulin-producing beta cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fever accelerates the renal clearance of her injected insulin doses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infection depletes hepatic glycogen stores and forces ketogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infection increases GLUT4 expression in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stress-induced glucocorticoids like cortisol alter insulin utilization

explanation.summary: Physical stressors such as infection raise glucocorticoids like cortisol that alter insulin utilization, precipitating DKA even with a strict insulin regimen.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to undiagnosed type 1 diabetes and missed insulin doses, DKA scenarios include patients with new stressors. Even patients following a strict insulin regimen can exhibit DKA upon introduction of physical burdens like infection, other acute illness, or emotional stress, because the resulting rise in glucocorticoids like cortisol alters insulin utilization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune loss of insulin production; infection-triggered DKA is explained by stress hormones, not toxin-mediated beta-cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Accelerated renal clearance of insulin is not the described mechanism for stress-precipitated DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DKA arises from ineffective insulin action and unrestrained fatty acid mobilization, not from glycogen depletion by infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased GLUT4 expression would enhance glucose uptake and oppose the starving state of DKA rather than cause it.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man in diabetic ketoacidosis complains of diffuse abdominal pain and nausea. His abdominal examination is unremarkable, and the pain resolves as the ketoacidosis is corrected. Besides the acidosis itself, which mechanism is proposed to contribute to his abdominal pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetone accumulating within the gastric and intestinal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adipose-derived prostaglandins causing vasodilation in the GI system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bile salt deficiency arising from reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eruptive xanthomas forming within the mesenteric fat deposits

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypoglycemia-driven vagal stimulation of the gut smooth muscle

explanation.summary: Prostaglandins released from overactive adipose tissue can cause vasodilation of organs including the GI system, contributing to abdominal pain in ketoacidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting are common in severe ketoacidosis and often resolve with its correction. Elevated prostaglandins may also play a role: they are released from overactive adipose tissue (which is breaking down triglycerides at a high rate) and can cause vasodilation of various organs, including in the GI system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetone is exhaled from the lungs, producing fruity breath; it is not described as depositing in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholesterol and bile salt synthesis are not implicated in the abdominal pain of ketoacidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eruptive xanthomas are cutaneous lesions of lipid disorders, not a cause of abdominal pain in DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DKA features an abundance of plasma glucose, not hypoglycemia, so this mechanism does not apply.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: Two patients present with ketoacidosis and a high anion gap. Patient 1 is a 50-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and malnutrition who has been drinking heavily for several days. Patient 2 is a 17-year-old with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes. Which finding most reliably distinguishes Patient 1's ketoacidosis from Patient 2's?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patient 1 has a low NADH:NAD+ ratio, whereas Patient 2 has a high one

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patient 1 has a normal anion gap, whereas Patient 2 has a high one

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patient 1 has fruity breath, whereas Patient 2 does not

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patient 1 is hypoglycemic, whereas Patient 2 is hyperglycemic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patient 1 lacks urinary ketones, whereas Patient 2 has them

explanation.summary: Alcoholic ketoacidosis is accompanied by hypoglycemia, whereas DKA occurs despite an abundance of glucose in the plasma.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic alcoholism, the NADH:NAD+ increase shunts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depriving gluconeogenesis of substrate; the combined effects produce hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis. In DKA, by contrast, insulin insufficiency leaves the body in a perceived starving state despite high extracellular glucose levels, so the ketoacidosis coexists with hyperglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol metabolism creates NADH and raises the NADH:NAD+ ratio in Patient 1; a low ratio is the opposite of what occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both conditions produce a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from accumulating ketone bodies (plus lactate in alcoholism).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fruity breath from exhaled acetone accompanies high ketone production in either condition and does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both patients have elevated ketones; ketone body levels rise in chronic alcoholism as well as in DKA.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man recently diagnosed with pre-diabetes based on his HbA1c starts a low-carbohydrate diet to lose 10% of his body weight. Over-the-counter urine strips show moderate ketones, and he is worried he is developing diabetic ketoacidosis. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His ketosis reflects fat breakdown, and his DKA risk is extremely low

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin should be started to suppress his ketone production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ketones on urine strips show that fat is not being broken down

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pre-diabetes carries the same DKA risk as untreated type 1 diabetes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary ketones signal DKA, so the diet must stop immediately

explanation.summary: Dietary ketosis is a natural response to fat breakdown and is not harmful; a pre-diabetic who still produces insulin has an extremely low risk of DKA.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pre-diabetic is becoming insulin resistant: he produces insulin but does not respond as effectively as he should. Ketone bodies are produced whenever fats are broken down in high amounts, and ketone production during prolonged fasting or low-glucose diets promotes weight reduction by fat loss, which aids someone who is insulin resistant. Urinalysis strips can monitor this natural response, which is not viewed as harmful. DKA, in stark contrast, results from insulin insufficiency in untreated type 1 (and select type 2) diabetes; his risk is extremely low.

whyWrongByChoice.B: He produces insulin and his ketosis is a benign dietary response; suppressing it with insulin is not indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ketones on urine strips are exactly the evidence that dietary practices are resulting in the breakdown of fats.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition with nominal insulin production; a pre-diabetic still produces insulin and has an extremely low DKA risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary ketones on a low-carbohydrate diet indicate fat breakdown, a natural dietary response, not DKA.

questions.topicName: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis and Ketone Bodies

questions.stem: After a wasp sting, a 30-year-old man develops local swelling and redness. Tissue-resident macrophages and infiltrating neutrophils release an enzyme that liberates the substrate for eicosanoid synthesis from the phospholipids of the cell membrane. Which of the following enzymes is directly responsible for releasing this substrate?

explanation.summary: PLA2 cleaves membrane phospholipids to release arachidonic acid, the substrate for eicosanoid synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In response to tissue damage, pro-inflammatory cells such as neutrophils and macrophages release phospholipase A2 (PLA2), which cleaves the sn-2 position of membrane phospholipids and liberates arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is the precursor from which all eicosanoids are subsequently generated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COX-1 acts downstream on arachidonic acid after it has already been released; it does not free the fatty acid from the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis and has no role in liberating arachidonic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LOX also acts downstream on already-released arachidonic acid to make leukotrienes, not on the membrane phospholipid itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phospholipase C generates lipid-derived second messengers that alter intracellular calcium levels; it does not release arachidonic acid for eicosanoid synthesis.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to characterize arachidonic acid, the key substrate of the inflammatory eicosanoid pathway. Which of the following best describes this molecule?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A phospholipid with a phosphate head group

choices.label: E
choices.text: A sterol with a four fused-ring structure

explanation.summary: Arachidonic acid is a 20-carbon omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid and the precursor of eicosanoids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arachidonic acid is a 20-carbon omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid that is an abundant membrane component. It is designated omega-6 because its first double bond occurs on the sixth carbon counting from the terminal methyl group, and its 20-carbon length is the origin of the term eicosanoid (Greek eicosa = 20).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arachidonic acid is unsaturated (it has multiple double bonds) and has 20 carbons, not 16, and it is not saturated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is an omega-6, not an omega-3, fatty acid; omega-3 species such as DHA have their first double bond on the third carbon from the methyl end.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arachidonic acid is a free fatty acid released from phospholipids, not a phospholipid bearing a phosphate head group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A four fused-ring structure describes cholesterol/sterols, not a fatty acid.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A researcher notes that a locally produced signaling molecule derived from arachidonic acid exerts its effect only near the cell that made it and disappears within minutes. Which property of eicosanoids best explains this restricted, short-range action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are covalently incorporated back into membrane phospholipids to provide long-term signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are G-protein coupled receptor ligands with a half-life of roughly 10 seconds to 5 minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are stored in secretory granules and released only in bulk after stimulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: They bind intracellular DNA response elements to alter gene transcription for hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: They circulate bound to albumin for several hours before acting on distant tissues

explanation.summary: Eicosanoids are short-lived GPCR ligands, so they act locally near their site of synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eicosanoids are ligands for G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) with a short half-life of 10 seconds to 5 minutes. Because they are rapidly degraded, they alter cellular function only within close proximity to where they are synthesized, giving them autocrine/paracrine (local) rather than endocrine (systemic) actions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are cleaved from membranes and act as diffusible ligands, not re-incorporated for long-term membrane signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eicosanoids are synthesized on demand from membrane arachidonic acid rather than pre-stored in granules for bulk release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eicosanoids act at cell-surface GPCRs, not by binding intracellular DNA elements like steroid hormones do.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Their very short half-life prevents prolonged circulation; they do not act systemically for hours.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: During an acute inflammatory response, a particular cyclooxygenase isoform is transiently expressed and drives the hallmarks of inflammation: pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Which enzyme is being described?

explanation.summary: COX-2 is the inducible isoform expressed during inflammation and tissue injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: COX-2 is referred to as the inducible form because it is transiently expressed during inflammation or tissue injury and is associated with the hallmarks of inflammation: pain, heat (fever), redness, and swelling. This distinction is the rationale behind developing selective COX-2 inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COX-1 is the constitutive form, continuously expressed to maintain physiological homeostasis, not transiently induced by inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LOX produces leukotrienes and is a separate branch; it is not the induced cyclooxygenase driving these classic inflammatory signs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PLA2 releases arachidonic acid upstream of COX and is not the inducible cyclooxygenase isoform.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane synthase converts PGH2 to thromboxane A2 and is not the inducible COX isoform associated with inflammation.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a recent mild stroke is started on low-dose daily aspirin for stroke and heart-attack prevention. Her lipid panel, LDL, HDL, and HMG-CoA reductase function are all unaffected by the drug. Which mechanism best explains aspirin's antithrombotic benefit in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of leukotriene receptors on platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase, lowering circulating LDL

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of phospholipase A2, reducing arachidonic acid release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible inhibition of platelet COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversible competitive inhibition of COX-2 in endothelium

explanation.summary: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1, abolishing thromboxane A2 production for the entire platelet lifespan.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelets are essentially anucleate cell fragments that lack organelles and cannot synthesize new protein. Once aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 in a platelet, thromboxane A2 (TXA2) production is blocked for the entire lifespan of that platelet. Reduced platelet-derived TXA2 decreases both platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, which is clinically beneficial in cardiovascular disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin acts on the COX enzyme, not on leukotriene receptors, and leukotrienes are not the antithrombotic mediator here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin does not affect HMG-CoA reductase or LDL; the vignette explicitly notes the lipid panel is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucocorticoids, not aspirin, inhibit PLA2; aspirin acts on COX downstream of arachidonic acid release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspirin inhibits COX irreversibly, not reversibly, and its antithrombotic effect is due to platelet COX-1, not endothelial COX-2.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Aspirin covalently modifies a serine residue in the active site of both cyclooxygenase isoforms, and this effect can only be overcome by synthesis of new enzyme. Which best describes this type of enzyme inhibition?

explanation.summary: Aspirin acetylates an active-site serine, irreversibly (suicide) inhibiting COX.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspirin promotes acetylation, a covalent post-translational modification, of a serine residue within the active site of both COX isoforms. This covalent modification irreversibly inhibits the enzyme by sterically blocking arachidonic acid entry into the active site, so the only way to overcome the inhibition is synthesis of new enzyme, making aspirin a suicide inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allosteric feedback inhibition is a reversible regulatory mechanism, not a covalent, irreversible modification of the active site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly and can be displaced by substrate; aspirin's covalent acetylation is not reversible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Noncompetitive inhibition is reversible and does not involve covalent modification of the active site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncompetitive inhibition binds only the enzyme-substrate complex reversibly and does not describe covalent acetylation.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with epigastric pain and bloating. He reports frequent ibuprofen use for chronic back pain over the past 8 months. Examination shows epigastric tenderness without rebound, and labs show mild normocytic anemia with no evidence of hemolysis. Which metabolic mechanism is most likely contributing to his condition?

explanation.summary: Chronic NSAID use inhibits COX-1, reducing protective gastric prostaglandins and predisposing to ulcers and bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged intake of an NSAID inhibits COX-1 and decreases production of prostaglandins such as PGE2 that are required for protective gastric mucus and reduced acid secretion. Loss of this mucosal protection leads to gastric bleeding and ulcers, a hallmark and major side effect of NSAID overuse, consistent with epigastric pain and a mild anemia from chronic blood loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COX inhibition would reduce, not increase, thromboxane A2; excess TXA2 does not cause gastric ulceration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inadequate erythrocyte NADPH causes hemolytic anemia (as in G6PD deficiency), but this patient has no evidence of hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PLA2 activity and arachidonic acid generation would not be enhanced by COX inhibition, and increased substrate does not account for the mucosal damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukotrienes are not associated with adverse GI effects; although excess arachidonic acid could be shunted to LOX, that would not explain the gastric injury.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A patient with a severe inflammatory condition is given a drug that broadly reduces production of prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes simultaneously by acting upstream in the arachidonic acid pathway. Which agent was most likely given?

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids inhibit PLA2, blocking arachidonic acid release and dampening both the COX and LOX branches.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucocorticoids such as cortisol and prednisone dampen inflammation by inhibiting the production of arachidonic acid via PLA2. Because arachidonic acid is the common substrate for both COX and LOX enzymes, blocking its release broadly suppresses prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes at once.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A leukotriene-receptor antagonist blocks only the LOX/leukotriene branch and does not reduce prostaglandins or thromboxanes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase to lower cholesterol synthesis and have no direct effect on the arachidonic acid pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspirin inhibits only the COX enzymes downstream of arachidonic acid; LOX-derived leukotrienes are not inhibited by COX blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ibuprofen also inhibits only COX, so it does not reduce leukotriene formation.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Several minutes after a bee sting, a patient who was given an antihistamine for immediate itching and hives develops worsening bronchoconstriction and inflammation that the antihistamine fails to control. This delayed but sustained reaction is mediated by molecules known as the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis. From which pathway are these mediators derived?

explanation.summary: Leukotrienes, the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis, are LOX-pathway products that cause delayed bronchoconstriction and inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes, which comprise the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A). Released from mast cells later than histamine and with a longer duration, leukotrienes cause pronounced bronchoconstriction and inflammation; because antihistamines do not block them, a steroid (which inhibits PLA2) is often warranted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The COX pathway produces prostaglandins and thromboxanes, not the leukotrienes that make up SRS-A.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The HMG-CoA reductase pathway is involved in cholesterol synthesis, not leukotriene production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate and has no role in eicosanoid synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The PLC pathway produces second messengers that raise intracellular calcium and does not generate leukotrienes.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: An obstetrician selects an eicosanoid agent to induce labor and to help manage postpartum hemorrhage by stimulating uterine contractions. Which mediator has these actions?

explanation.summary: PGE2 stimulates uterine contractions, aiding labor induction and management of postpartum hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the eicosanoids, PGE2 promotes labor induction and helps manage postpartum hemorrhage by stimulating uterine contractions. This reproductive role is one of the many physiological effects of prostaglandins produced through the COX pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arachidonic acid is the upstream fatty acid precursor and has no direct receptor-mediated uterotonic action itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukotriene B4 is a LOX product that drives leukocyte chemotaxis and inflammation, not uterine contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostacyclin (PGI2) inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates blood vessels; it is not used to stimulate uterine contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, not uterine contraction for labor induction.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A cardiologist explains that low-dose aspirin permanently disables thromboxane production in platelets, yet vascular endothelial cells continue to make vasodilatory prostaglandins over time. Which feature of endothelial cells best explains their ability to overcome aspirin's inhibition and keep producing PGI2 and PGE2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin binds endothelial COX reversibly but platelet COX irreversibly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial cells contain organelles and can translate new COX-2 enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothelial cells convert thromboxane A2 into prostacyclin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endothelial cells lack COX enzymes entirely

choices.label: E
choices.text: Endothelial cells use LOX instead of COX to make prostaglandins

explanation.summary: Because endothelial cells have organelles, they can synthesize new COX-2 and overcome aspirin's irreversible inhibition, unlike anucleate platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike platelets, organelle-containing endothelial cells can translate new COX-2 enzyme, which overcomes the aspirin-mediated inhibition. This restored COX-2 produces PGE2 and PGI2, both of which promote vasodilation. Low-dose aspirin is chosen so that platelet COX-1 is permanently disabled while endothelial COX-2 can regenerate, forming the basis of low-dose aspirin therapy to lower stroke and heart-attack risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin inhibits COX irreversibly in both cell types; the difference is that endothelium can make new enzyme while platelets cannot.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no enzymatic conversion of thromboxane A2 into prostacyclin; PGI2 is synthesized directly from the PGH2 precursor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endothelial cells do express COX (notably COX-2); they do not lack the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins including PGI2 are made by COX, not LOX; LOX makes leukotrienes.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A patient with an inflammatory disorder that has not responded to other agents is prescribed indomethacin, a very potent NSAID. Compared with aspirin, how does indomethacin inhibit cyclooxygenase, and why does it tend to cause more gastric side effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Irreversible acetylation of COX; more gastric effects from higher COX-2 affinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irreversible inhibition of LOX; more gastric effects from increased prostaglandins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reversible competitive inhibition of COX; more gastric effects from higher COX-1 affinity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversible inhibition of PLA2; more gastric effects from reduced leukotrienes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective irreversible inhibition of COX-2 only; more gastric effects from blocked PGI2

explanation.summary: Indomethacin is a reversible competitive COX inhibitor with higher affinity for COX-1, accounting for its greater gastric toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike aspirin, indomethacin is not a suicide inhibitor; it is a very potent reversible, competitive COX inhibitor. Although it inhibits both isoforms, indomethacin has a higher affinity for COX-1, and greater COX-1 inhibition reduces the protective gastric prostaglandins, which accounts for its increased adverse gastric effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Irreversible acetylation describes aspirin, not indomethacin; and gastric toxicity relates to COX-1, not COX-2, inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Indomethacin inhibits COX, not LOX, and it decreases rather than increases prostaglandin production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Indomethacin inhibits COX, not PLA2, and its gastric effects stem from loss of protective prostaglandins, not reduced leukotrienes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Indomethacin is not a COX-2 selective agent; loss of protective gastric prostaglandins comes from COX-1, not blocked PGI2 alone.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A biochemist incubates a membrane glycerophospholipid, which has fatty acids esterified at carbons 1 and 2 of glycerol, a phosphate on carbon 3, and a polar head group attached to that phosphate, with a purified phospholipase. Analysis shows the head group has been cleaved off while the phosphate remains attached to the glycerol backbone. Which enzyme was used?

explanation.summary: Phospholipase D cleaves the bond between the phosphate and the polar head group of a membrane phospholipid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Distinct phospholipases cleave membrane lipids at distinct sites. Phospholipase D acts on the phosphate-head group bond, releasing the head group and leaving the phosphate attached to carbon 3 of the glycerol backbone. Its functions, along with those of PLA1, are covered in later courses, but its site of action is distinct from PLA1, PLA2, and PLC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipoxygenase acts on free arachidonic acid to form leukotrienes; it does not cleave membrane phospholipids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phospholipase A1 cleaves the ester bond joining the fatty acid to carbon 1 of glycerol, not the head-group bond.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phospholipase A2 cleaves the ester bond at carbon 2, releasing the fatty acid (such as arachidonic acid) at that position.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase C cleaves between carbon 3 of glycerol and the phosphate, so the phosphate would leave with the head group rather than stay on the backbone.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A hormone binds its cell-surface receptor and activates a membrane phospholipase that cleaves the bond between the glycerol backbone and the phosphate group of a phospholipid. The resulting lipid-derived mediators alter intracellular Ca++ levels. Which enzyme was activated?

explanation.summary: Phospholipase C cleaves between glycerol and phosphate, generating lipid-derived mediators of cell signaling that alter intracellular calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phospholipase C (PLC) acts at the bond between carbon 3 of the glycerol backbone and the phosphate. Its products are lipid-derived second messengers that alter intracellular Ca++ levels, a signaling role distinct from the inflammatory pathway that depends on PLA2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyclooxygenase-2 converts already-released arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2; it does not cleave membrane phospholipids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phospholipase A1 removes the fatty acid esterified at carbon 1 of glycerol and is not the source of calcium-altering messengers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phospholipase A2 cleaves the fatty acid at carbon 2 to release arachidonic acid for the inflammatory eicosanoid cascade, not calcium-altering mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phospholipase D cleaves between the phosphate and the head group, on the far side of the phosphate from the glycerol backbone.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has followed a strict diet for 5 years that excludes meat, eggs, and fish. Despite consuming no dietary arachidonic acid, her cell membranes contain normal amounts of it. Arachidonic acid is most likely being synthesized in her body from which of the following?

explanation.summary: Arachidonic acid can be obtained from animal foods or synthesized from linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dietary sources of arachidonic acid include animal-based foods such as meat, eggs, and fish, but arachidonic acid can also be synthesized from linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid that must come from the diet. This endogenous route maintains membrane arachidonic acid even when animal foods are excluded.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholesterol is a four-ring sterol, not a fatty acid, and is not a precursor of arachidonic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Docosahexaenoic acid is an omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid found in fish; it is not the precursor of the omega-6 arachidonic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin H2 is a product formed downstream of arachidonic acid by COX, not a source of it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is an eicosanoid product derived from arachidonic acid, not a precursor.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old hiker is bitten on the leg by a snake. Within an hour he develops rapidly spreading swelling, severe pain, tissue damage, and impaired blood clotting at the bite site. Which component of the venom most directly triggers this catastrophic inflammatory response?

choices.label: B
choices.text: HMG-CoA reductase that raises cholesterol output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phospholipase A2 that liberates arachidonic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Steroid molecules that diffuse into host cells

explanation.summary: Bee and snake venoms contain high levels of active PLA2, which drives acute, catastrophic inflammation in the victim.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many types of venom contain high levels of active phospholipase A2. Injected PLA2 releases arachidonic acid from the victim's membrane lipids, driving acute, catastrophic inflammation. In snakes, venom injection immobilizes prey through inflammatory-mediated tissue toxicities and disruption of blood coagulation, matching this patient's tissue damage and clotting abnormality.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COX-2 is an inducible host enzyme acting downstream of arachidonic acid; it is not the venom component the brick describes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HMG-CoA reductase governs cholesterol synthesis and plays no role in the inflammatory cascade triggered by venom.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoxygenase is a host enzyme downstream of arachidonic acid release; venom toxicity is attributed to its high PLA2 content.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steroids that diffuse into cells describe glucocorticoids, which dampen rather than provoke inflammation.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A student is asked to classify an unsaturated fatty acid as omega-3 or omega-6. In this nomenclature, which carbon of the fatty acid is counted as carbon #1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The carbon at the exact midpoint of the hydrocarbon chain

choices.label: B
choices.text: The carbon bearing the first double bond nearest the methyl end

choices.label: C
choices.text: The carbon immediately adjacent to the carboxyl group

choices.label: D
choices.text: The carbon of the carboxylic acid group at the oxidized end

choices.label: E
choices.text: The terminal methyl carbon farthest from the carboxyl group

explanation.summary: Omega numbering starts at the terminal methyl carbon farthest from the carboxylic acid, the reverse of IUPAC numbering.
explanation.whyCorrect: Omega is the terminal letter of the Greek alphabet and denotes the terminal carbon in the fatty acid chain farthest from the most oxidized end (the carboxylic acid). Numbering begins at this methyl end rather than the carboxyl end, which is the reverse of the IUPAC priorities used in organic chemistry. The number 3 or 6 then designates where the first double bond occurs as if the omega carbon were #1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The midpoint of the chain has no role in either omega or IUPAC numbering.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first double bond's position is what the omega number reports; it is not the starting point for counting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group is near the oxidized end, whereas omega counting starts at the methyl end.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The carboxylic acid carbon is carbon #1 in IUPAC nomenclature, but omega numbering deliberately starts at the opposite end.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A polyunsaturated fatty acid enriched in tuna and salmon is drawn with a single carboxylic acid group, no ring structures, and six double bonds, the first of which occurs on the third carbon counting from the terminal methyl group. Which of the following best identifies this molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arachidonic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Docosahexaenoic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linoleic acid, an essential omega-6 fatty acid

explanation.summary: DHA is an omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid enriched in fish such as tuna and salmon.
explanation.whyCorrect: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is an omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid enriched in meat sources such as tuna and salmon. It is a fatty acid (carboxylic acid with a hydrocarbon chain), it is unsaturated because it contains multiple double bonds, and it is omega-3 because the first double bond occurs on the 3rd carbon away from the terminal carbon farthest from the carboxylic acid end.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arachidonic acid is an omega-6 fatty acid, meaning its first double bond is on the 6th carbon from the methyl end, not the 3rd.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholesterol has a signature four fused-ring structure, which this molecule lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linoleic acid is the essential fatty acid precursor of arachidonic acid, not the omega-3 fatty acid enriched in fish.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandin H2 is a downstream COX product of arachidonic acid, not a dietary omega-3 fatty acid.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man eats a diet high in red meat, processed food, and sugar and low in fish, nuts, and legumes. Nutritional analysis shows a markedly elevated omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acid ratio. Which of the following best explains why this ratio may favor a pro-inflammatory state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arachidonic acid, an omega-6 precursor of eicosanoids, is enriched

choices.label: B
choices.text: Omega-3 fatty acids induce COX-2 expression in tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Omega-3 fatty acids serve as the precursor of thromboxane A2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Omega-6 fatty acids block leukotriene receptors on mast cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omega-6 fatty acids inhibit phospholipase A2 in immune cells

explanation.summary: An elevated omega-6 to omega-3 ratio enriches arachidonic acid, the omega-6 precursor of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arachidonic acid is an omega-6 fatty acid and the precursor to molecules in the pro-inflammatory cascade. When the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio is elevated, arachidonic acid is enriched, favoring a pro-inflammatory state. This is why adding omega-3 fatty acids, as in the Mediterranean diet (limiting red meat, processed food, and sugar while adding fish, nuts, seeds, legumes, and produce), is encouraged.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Omega-3 enrichment is encouraged to counter inflammation; it is not described as inducing COX-2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thromboxane A2 is derived from arachidonic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid, not from omega-3 fatty acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Omega-6 fatty acids have no receptor-blocking action on leukotrienes; leukotriene-receptor antagonists are drugs used in asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Omega-6 fatty acids do not inhibit PLA2; they are the source of the arachidonic acid PLA2 releases.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Both COX-1 and COX-2 act on arachidonic acid to generate a single common intermediate that is subsequently converted into the various prostaglandins and thromboxanes. Which of the following is that intermediate?

explanation.summary: COX-1 and COX-2 both convert arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2, the common precursor of prostaglandins and thromboxanes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both COX isoforms cleave arachidonic acid into the common prostaglandin H2 precursor. PGH2 is then further converted into the other prostaglandins (PGs) such as PGE2, PGF2 alpha, and PGI2, or into thromboxanes (TXs) such as TXA2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukotrienes are formed from arachidonic acid by lipoxygenase, an entirely separate branch from COX.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prostacyclin (PGI2) is a prostaglandin generated from PGH2, not the common intermediate itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostaglandin E2 is one of the end products made from PGH2, not the shared intermediate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is a downstream product derived from PGH2, not the precursor.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman sprains her ankle and reports throbbing pain at the injury site. Which pair of eicosanoids directly stimulates pain receptors in this setting?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prostaglandin F2 alpha and prostaglandin E2

explanation.summary: PGF2 alpha and PGE2 both stimulate pain receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the COX-derived mediators, PGF2 alpha and PGE2 both stimulate pain receptors, accounting for the pain that accompanies inflammation. This is one reason COX-inhibiting NSAIDs relieve pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukotrienes mediate allergic responses and chemotaxis, and thromboxane A2 acts on platelets and vessels, not pain receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prostacyclin inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates vessels, and PGH2 is the common precursor rather than the pain mediator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PGH2 is the intermediate converted to other mediators, and thromboxane A2 acts on platelets and vasculature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, and prostacyclin inhibits aggregation; neither is listed as a pain-receptor stimulator.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Which eicosanoid, produced by COX-2 in vascular endothelium, both inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates blood vessels, thereby opposing the actions of thromboxane A2?

explanation.summary: PGI2 (prostacyclin) inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates vessels, the opposite of TXA2.
explanation.whyCorrect: PGI2, also known as prostacyclin, inhibits platelet aggregation, whereas TXA2 causes platelet aggregation and clot formation. PGI2 (together with PGE2) also dilates blood vessels through the action of COX-2 in vascular endothelium, while TXA2 made via COX-1 in platelets constricts the vasculature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukotrienes are LOX products involved in allergic responses, inflammation, and chemotaxis, not platelet inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PGF2 alpha stimulates pain receptors; it is not described as inhibiting platelets or dilating vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin H2 is the common precursor that is converted into PGI2 and other mediators; it is not the active antiplatelet vasodilator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is the mediator being opposed; it causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: An investigator studying bone homeostasis observes that adding PGE2 to a bone culture increases bone resorption. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which PGE2 promotes resorption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PGE2 directly stimulates osteoclasts to dissolve bone matrix

choices.label: B
choices.text: PGE2 recruits neutrophils into bone through chemotaxis

choices.label: C
choices.text: PGE2 stimulates osteoblasts to release factors that activate osteoclasts

choices.label: D
choices.text: PGE2 stimulates osteoclasts to release factors that inhibit osteoblasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: PGE2 suppresses osteoblast synthesis of new bone matrix

explanation.summary: PGE2 acts on osteoblasts, which release factors that promote bone resorption by osteoclasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: In bone homeostasis, PGE2 stimulates osteoblasts to release factors that promote bone resorption by osteoclasts. The effect on resorption is therefore indirect: the bone-forming osteoblast is the PGE2 target, and its released factors drive the bone-resorbing osteoclast.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes PGE2 acting on osteoblasts, which then signal to osteoclasts, rather than a direct osteoclast effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemotaxis of neutrophils is a leukotriene action from the LOX pathway, not the PGE2 mechanism in bone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The direction is reversed: osteoblasts release the factors and osteoclasts carry out resorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PGE2 is described as stimulating osteoblasts to release factors, not as suppressing their matrix synthesis.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company invests heavily in designing a drug that selectively inhibits COX-2 while sparing COX-1. Which adverse effect of nonselective COX inhibitors is this design principally intended to circumvent?

explanation.summary: Selective COX-2 inhibitors were developed to avoid the gastric ulcers and bleeding caused by inhibiting constitutive COX-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged inhibition of COX enzymes leads to gastric ulcers and bleeding because of a lack of prostaglandins required for protective gastric secretions. Much research effort has been spent developing selective COX-2 inhibitors to circumvent these adverse effects of inhibiting COX-1 by more strategically targeting the inducible isoform associated with pain and inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoconstriction is a leukotriene-mediated effect of the LOX pathway, which COX inhibitors do not block in either direction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disrupted glucose homeostasis is a pleiotropic glucocorticoid side effect, not an NSAID gastric problem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated blood pressure is listed as a side effect of glucocorticoids, not the COX-1-related toxicity that COX-2 selectivity targets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uterine contraction is a physiological PGE2 action used for labor induction, not the adverse effect COX-2 selectivity was designed to avoid.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic joint inflammation took rofecoxib (Vioxx), a COX-2 specific inhibitor, for 2 years before the manufacturer withdrew it from the market. Such agents were associated with adverse cardiovascular events. Which of the following best explains this association?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of PLA2 with reduced arachidonic acid release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible acetylation of platelet COX-1 blocking thromboxane A2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of COX-1-derived PGE2 that protects the gastric mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of endothelial COX-2 prostaglandins required for vasodilation

explanation.summary: COX-2 in vascular endothelium makes PGE2 and PGI2 needed for vasodilation, so selective COX-2 inhibition is linked to adverse cardiovascular events.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostaglandins derived from COX enzymes are required for vasodilation; PGE2 and PGI2 dilate blood vessels through the action of COX-2 in vascular endothelium. Because a COX-2 specific inhibitor removes these vasodilatory mediators, adverse cardiovascular events have been associated with select COX inhibitors, culminating in Merck's removal of Vioxx (rofecoxib) from the market.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukotriene chemotaxis belongs to the LOX pathway, which is not typically affected by COX inhibitors and does not explain the cardiovascular risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PLA2 inhibition is the mechanism of glucocorticoids, not of a COX-2 specific inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irreversible acetylation of platelet COX-1 is aspirin's mechanism and is antithrombotic and cardioprotective, not the harm attributed to a COX-2 specific agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of gastric protective prostaglandins is the COX-1 toxicity that COX-2 selectivity was designed to avoid, not a cardiovascular effect.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Histologic examination of an acutely inflamed tissue reveals large numbers of neutrophils that have migrated toward and adhered at the site of injury. Which arachidonic acid-derived mediators promote this migration (chemotaxis) and adhesion of immune cells?

explanation.summary: Select leukotrienes, made by lipoxygenase, increase chemotaxis and adhesion of immune cells such as neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alternative to COX enzymes, arachidonic acid can be converted by LOX enzymes to form leukotrienes. Leukotrienes are mediators of the allergic response and inflammation, and select leukotrienes increase the migration (chemotaxis) and adhesion of immune cells like neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prostacyclin inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates vessels; it is not the chemotactic mediator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostaglandin H2 is the common precursor converted into other prostaglandins and thromboxanes, not a chemotactic signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: COX-1-derived prostaglandins maintain physiological homeostasis; chemotaxis is attributed to leukotrienes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxanes cause platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction rather than immune-cell chemotaxis.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman takes high doses of ibuprofen daily for chronic joint pain. Which of the following arachidonic acid-derived mediators would be expected to be unchanged or even increased, rather than decreased, by this medication?

explanation.summary: LOX enzymes are not typically inhibited by COX-inhibiting drugs, so leukotriene production persists and may rise as excess arachidonic acid is shunted to LOX.
explanation.whyCorrect: Importantly, LOX enzymes are not typically inhibited by medications that inhibit COX function. When COX is blocked by an NSAID such as ibuprofen, arachidonic acid is no longer converted by COX, and the excess arachidonic acid might be utilized by LOX enzymes instead, so leukotriene production is maintained or increased while all COX products fall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prostacyclin is a COX-2-derived prostaglandin and is reduced by ibuprofen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostaglandin E2 is a COX product downstream of PGH2 and falls when COX is inhibited.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin H2 is the direct product of COX acting on arachidonic acid, so its formation is blocked by the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboxane A2 is formed from the COX product PGH2 and decreases with COX inhibition.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with asthma is prescribed a maintenance medication that blocks the receptor for the lipoxygenase-derived eicosanoids responsible for bronchoconstriction. To which class does this drug belong?

explanation.summary: LOX inhibitors and leukotriene-receptor antagonists are used to treat select forms of asthma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukotrienes formed by LOX enzymes mediate allergic responses and cause pronounced bronchoconstriction. LOX inhibitors and LT-receptor antagonists are therefore used to treat select forms of asthma; a drug that blocks the leukotriene receptor is an LT-receptor antagonist.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines treat the immediate histamine reaction but fail to prevent the later leukotriene response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) suppress endogenous cholesterol production and have no role in asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An irreversible COX inhibitor such as aspirin acts on the COX branch; LOX products are not affected by COX inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A selective COX-2 inhibitor targets prostaglandin synthesis and does not block leukotriene receptors.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Corticosteroids are steroid hormones produced in the adrenal cortex or made synthetically and are divided into two classes based on action. A patient is given a corticosteroid that influences salt and water balance but provides no anti-inflammatory benefit. To which class does this agent belong?

explanation.summary: Mineralocorticoids are corticosteroids that regulate salt and water balance and are not anti-inflammatory.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids are divided into glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids. Mineralocorticoids, while a type of corticosteroid, are not anti-inflammatory in nature but rather influence salt and water balance. Only glucocorticoids dampen inflammation by inhibiting PLA2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucocorticoids such as cortisol and prednisone are the anti-inflammatory corticosteroid class that inhibits PLA2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukotriene-receptor antagonists are asthma drugs that block LOX-pathway mediators, not corticosteroids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NSAIDs are not corticosteroids at all; they are nonsteroidal drugs that inhibit COX enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins are HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors that lower cholesterol synthesis, not adrenal steroid hormones.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman treated with prednisone for 6 months for an inflammatory disorder develops weight gain, elevated blood pressure, disrupted glucose homeostasis, and "jitters." Which property of this drug class best accounts for such widespread (pleiotropic) effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As steroid-based agents, they readily diffuse into cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: They act only at surface GPCRs with a short half-life

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase in hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: They irreversibly acetylate COX-1 within platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: They selectively induce COX-2 in vascular endothelium

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids readily diffuse into cells and prompt varied physiological responses, producing pleiotropic side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucocorticoids prompt varied physiological responses, so their use is associated with unwanted, deleterious side effects. As steroid-based agents, they readily diffuse into cells, further causing undesired responses. These pleiotropic effects on the body result in weight gain, jitters, disrupted glucose homeostasis, and elevated blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Short-lived action at cell-surface GPCRs describes eicosanoids themselves, not steroid drugs that enter cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is the action of statins on cholesterol synthesis, unrelated to prednisone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irreversible acetylation of platelet COX-1 is the mechanism of aspirin, not of glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucocorticoids dampen inflammation by inhibiting PLA2 upstream; they do not induce COX-2.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Aspirin inactivates COX by transferring its acetyl group onto a serine residue in the enzyme's active site. After this transfer, which molecule remains from the drug?

explanation.summary: When aspirin acetylates the COX active-site serine, the remaining portion of the drug is salicylic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspirin is an acetylated form of salicylic acid, the active substance originally isolated from willow bark and chemically modified for palatability and reactivity. Aspirin donates its acetyl group to the serine side chain in the polypeptide of COX-1 and COX-2, producing acetylated (irreversibly inhibited) COX and leaving salicylic acid behind.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arachidonic acid is the substrate whose entry into the active site is sterically blocked after acetylation; it is not derived from aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisone is a glucocorticoid that inhibits PLA2 and has no chemical relationship to aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ibuprofen is a separate NSAID that inhibits COX reversibly and competitively; it is not generated from aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin H2 is the COX product that can no longer be made once the enzyme is acetylated.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Ancient civilizations, including the Greeks and Native Americans, used willow bark for its therapeutic effects. Scientists later isolated the active substance, chemically modified it for palatability and reactivity, and marketed it cheaply. Which drug resulted?

explanation.summary: Aspirin derives from salicylic acid, the therapeutic substance in willow bark, and remains one of the cheapest, most widely used drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspirin remains one of the most widely used and cheapest drugs globally. Its origins lie with individuals who long preceded modern medicine and recognized the therapeutic property within willow bark. Scientists later isolated the active substance, salicylic acid, chemically modified it for palatability and reactivity, and marketed it cheaply.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ibuprofen is another reversible, competitive COX inhibitor and is not the willow-bark derivative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Indomethacin is a potent reversible, competitive COX inhibitor with no origin in willow bark.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone is a synthetic glucocorticoid that inhibits PLA2, not a salicylate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rofecoxib (Vioxx) was a COX-2 specific inhibitor developed by Merck and later withdrawn; it is unrelated to willow bark.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A physician prescribes a daily low-dose ("baby") aspirin, rather than a standard anti-inflammatory dose, to a 70-year-old woman after a mild stroke. Which of the following best describes the strategic rationale for choosing the low dose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: COX-2 is selectively acetylated while COX-1 in platelets is spared

choices.label: B
choices.text: HMG-CoA reductase is partially inhibited, lowering LDL cholesterol

choices.label: C
choices.text: PLA2 is inhibited upstream so both COX and LOX products fall together

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet COX-1 is only reversibly inhibited so thromboxane recovers quickly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet COX-1 is permanently inhibited while endothelial COX-2 is not fully inhibited

explanation.summary: Low-dose aspirin permanently disables platelet COX-1 but is ineffective at fully inhibiting endothelial COX-2, preserving vasodilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The recommended dose of aspirin is strategic: COX-1 enzymes within platelets that promote clot formation and vasoconstriction are permanently inhibited, but the small dose is ineffective at fully inhibiting the COX-2 enzymes within vascular endothelium that promote vasodilation. COX-2 is still inhibited to a degree, but the small dosing allows the inhibition to be overcome in endothelium through expression of more COX-2, whereas platelets cannot express more COX-1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin acetylates both COX isoforms; the selectivity comes from dose and cell biology, not from sparing COX-1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin does not alter cholesterol synthesis, HMG-CoA reductase function, or LDL production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PLA2 inhibition is the mechanism of glucocorticoids; aspirin acts on COX downstream of arachidonic acid release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspirin inhibits COX irreversibly at any dose; platelet thromboxane does not recover because platelets cannot make new enzyme.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man on daily low-dose aspirin for stroke prevention asks whether he can substitute daily ibuprofen, which he already takes for knee pain. Which of the following best explains why ibuprofen is not used as a prophylactic antithrombotic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ibuprofen cannot diffuse into anucleate platelets, so platelet COX-1 is never reached

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ibuprofen inhibits COX reversibly, so platelet TXA2 synthesis resumes as drug clears

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ibuprofen inhibits lipoxygenase rather than cyclooxygenase enzymes in platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ibuprofen inhibits PLA2 upstream of COX, leaving thromboxane synthesis intact

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ibuprofen selectively inhibits COX-2 and spares the platelet COX-1 isoform

explanation.summary: Aspirin is the only NSAID that irreversibly inhibits COX; reversible inhibitors like ibuprofen cannot permanently disable platelet thromboxane production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspirin is the only NSAID that irreversibly inhibits COX enzymes, which allows it to be uniquely used as a prophylactic antithrombotic: once platelet COX-1 is acetylated, TXA2 production is blocked for the entirety of the platelet's life span. Ibuprofen, like indomethacin, is a reversible, competitive COX inhibitor, so its inhibition is not permanent and platelet TXA2 production can resume.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ibuprofen does reach and inhibit COX in platelets; the issue is that the inhibition is reversible rather than permanent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ibuprofen is a COX inhibitor; LOX enzymes are not typically inhibited by COX-blocking medications.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PLA2 inhibition is the mechanism of glucocorticoids, not NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ibuprofen is a nonselective COX inhibitor, not a COX-2 specific agent like rofecoxib.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: Under basal, non-inflamed conditions, a healthy person's tissues continuously produce prostaglandins that maintain physiological homeostasis. Which enzyme is responsible for this constitutive production?

explanation.summary: COX-1 is the constitutive isoform, continuously expressed to maintain body homeostasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The COX enzyme exists in two isoforms. COX-1 is referred to as the constitutive form, the form continuously expressed to maintain body homeostasis, and it helps maintain physiological homeostasis such as protective gastric secretions and platelet thromboxane production.

whyWrongByChoice.B: COX-2 is the inducible isoform, transiently expressed during inflammation or tissue injury rather than under basal conditions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes, not the homeostatic prostaglandins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase C generates calcium-altering second messengers and does not produce prostaglandins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phospholipase D cleaves the phospholipid head group and does not make prostaglandins.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction (3 of 3)

questions.stem: A patient with a severe allergic reaction receives intravenous cortisol. Beyond dampening inflammation and influencing metabolism, which of the following vascular effects is characteristic of glucocorticoids?

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids influence metabolism, dampen inflammatory processes, and cause vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucocorticoids are the corticosteroid class that influences metabolism, dampens inflammatory processes, and causes vasoconstriction. Their anti-inflammatory action comes from inhibiting PLA2, but the vasoconstrictive effect is a separate characteristic action of the class, consistent with the elevated blood pressure seen as a side effect of prolonged use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoconstriction is caused by leukotrienes; glucocorticoids dampen leukotriene formation by inhibiting PLA2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet aggregation is an action of thromboxane A2 made by platelet COX-1, not an effect of glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Uterine contraction is a PGE2 action used in labor induction, not a glucocorticoid effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasodilation via prostacyclin is a COX-2-dependent prostaglandin effect; glucocorticoids reduce eicosanoid production and cause vasoconstriction.
